Our findings indicate that cosmic rays exhibit significant anisotropies on an enormous scale above 4 EeV, with the Pierre Auger Observatory revealing key patterns. When considering sources more distant than 75 million light-years, a spatial anisotropy became apparent, with a 3 sigma level of confidence. Specifically, there are areas of enhanced and diminished cosmic-ray density located at right ascensions 339° and 306°, spanning approximately 12° in width. The density variations amount to a 4 sigma level of confidence. To further elucidate these anisotropies, we undertook a comprehensive statistical analysis across the celestial sphere, employing four distinct methods to control for multiple comparisons. All analysis techniques consistently identified the primary anisotropy features mentioned above. Moreover, we observed a secondary anisotropy at a 2 sigma level of confidence, influenced by the direction of the Large Magellanic Cloud. The anisotropy patterns exhibited little variation when accounting for the orientation of the cosmic-ray arrival orientations, known as the "alignment gap" effect. The anisotropy features also demonstrated little dependence on primary particle types, such as protons, helium nuclei, and nitrogene nuclei, above 4 EeV. The statistical analysis employed real-space and Fourier transforms to identify the anisotropy patterns. To interpret our findings, we considered several theoretical frameworks commonly used to model cosmic-ray sources, including the generic "extragalactic cosmic-ray cascade" model and two specific variants, as well as a "local source" model. Our data provided new constraints for model predictions, with some models failing to replicate the observed anisotropy patterns, while others matched our observations with a 2 sigma level of confidence. Our research highlights the importance of continued wide-scale detection of cosmic rays to confirm and refine our anisotropy findings. Systematic systematic biases identified in our study suggest appropriate adjustments for in situ cosmic-ray detectors such as the Pierre Auger Observatory's underground detectors. Our analysis revealed that a previously reported "Octant" study contained a single event in common, which is significant because that study reported different anisotropy patterns. Our study also compared our anisotropy findings to those from two recent analyses of data collected by the Telescope Array, with the latter showing a similar spatial anisotropy feature and density variation. In the harmonic oscillator case, we show that all deformed Hamiltonian operators equivalent to the Poisson bracket can be expressed as a linear combination of the unit operator and the deformed number operator, resulting in the exact commutation of these operators. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, providing an extensive platform for users to leverage its content and the Isabelle community for support. To facilitate a deeper understanding of the archive's structure and effectiveness, we have developed a comprehensive analysis framework that showcases its intricate design. By exploring various aspects of the archive, our study aims to enhance the user experience and the community's collaborative efforts within Isabelle. To this end, we have created a simplified replication pathway for full-scale proofs, making it easier for users to modify existing content. Additionally, we have introduced a rating system that assesses the clarity of text within the archive, providing valuable insights for the Isabelle community to focus on improving the comprehensibility of its documentation. Moreover, our analysis has inspired the creation of Isabelle Proof Generalisation, a new tool enabling users to automate the generalisation of proofs from specific theories to more general ones. This innovative approach has already been applied in enhancing the archive's content, and we anticipate it to have broad applications in the Isabelle environment. By generalising proofs, users can quickly leverage the archive's content to develop new results in mathematics and computer science, thereby contributing to the continued growth and diversity of the archive. With this analysis and new functionality, we aim to elevate the user experience within the archive, facilitate the discovery of relevant content, and provide a more effective platform for users to explore and interact with the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. Furthermore, we have explored multiple pathways for integrating the archive with the Isabelle community, involving the development of tailored refinements of the Uniform Proofs framework, specifically tailored to the archive's purposes. By combining the archive with the expertise of the Isabelle community, we have created opportunities for both users and the community to benefit from the archive's content, the community's collective knowledge, and the collective experience of the Isabelle community, thereby elevating the archive to a position where it can provide uniform proofs for any mathematical theorem. In recognition of the significant progress made available by the archive and the community, we have introduced the Isabelle Archive Community Award, honouring the archive and the community for their groundbreaking work, and we have established the Isabelle Proofs Hall of Fame to celebrate the most renowned proofs developed using Isabelle, incorporating the award-winning uniform proofs from the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation Potential Network (eCPN), which can learn simplified potential functions that accurately capture the complex behavior of electron interactions within atoms and molecules. Trained in an unsupervised manner with correlated wave functions, eCPN can efficiently model the behavior of electrons by limiting their degrees of freedom. Our results demonstrate eCPN's capability to model intermediate to strongly correlated systems with great precision, surpassing traditional mean-field theories in its level of accuracy as the level of electron interaction increases. Furthermore, we found eCPN's potential to significantly improve the convergence rates of correlated calculations, particularly in scenarios where electrons exhibit strong interactions. As such, eCPN presents an exciting opportunity for correlated electron studies, potentially enabling the advancement to complete configuration interaction (CCI) approaches that consider all possible electron permutations. Our data also reveals the role of neural network depth in achieving optimal correlation results, with trade-offs existing between the complexity of electron description, training stability, and computational cost. Ultimately, we believe the eCPN framework can facilitate the exploration of complex electronic situations that have historically posed challenges to theoretical description. With its successful application to benchmark tests including ground-state energies, occupation numbers, and molecular potentials, eCPN is now poised to analyze important phenomena arising from the intricate interactions of electrons. As such, we plan to investigate pivotal issues in chemistry and physics using the eCPN tool, with attention being paid to implementing eCPN within a correlated workflow that leverages the resources of high-performance computational systems. Recently, modern pose estimation methods on the COCO dataset have achieved near optimal results with low axes of variation, but significant challenges remain with frequently occurring poses that have complex shapes. A key issue in solving this problem is the initial representation of objects, as many existing approaches often start with feature extraction using convolutional neural networks, resulting in abstract representations that can lead to pose estimation ambiguities. In contrast, this paper takes a unique starting point, employing a fully trained network to establish correspondence between 2D images and 3D models through clustering, with an emphasis on preserving key facial features. By utilizing 3D models with numerous distinctive landmarks, this approach enables direct comparison of images in real numbers, as opposed to comparison in the projective plane. To overcome challenges like translation, rotation, and projection ambiguities, this paper introduces an innovative distortion-invariant metric and minimization framework, allowing for efficient optimization using the conjugate gradient method. Extensive experiments on the CFP (Frontal) and AFW (frontal/subfrontal) subsets of the COCO dataset demonstrate the superiority of this method over state-of-the-art pose estimation approaches. Furthermore, this paper explores how clustering impacts modeling faces with various shapes and identities, incorporating the Reunion dataset to examine these effects. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zwang84/DeepHMap/blob/main/README.md. With significant improvements achieved on the CFP/AFW subsets of the COCO dataset and frontally posed faces in the Reunion and VGGFace2 datasets, this project particularly outperforms state-of-the-art methods like DeepPoseRT and OpenPose RT on the CFP/AFW subsets. On these specific datasets, this research introduces novel applications of projection clustering, correspondence learning, and a groundbreaking real-number comparison approach. Additionally, a follow-up study is currently being developed for extending this method to estimate hands. Open-source code for this project is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/DeepHMap/commits/main. With numerous face detection methods capable of identifying faces with wide variations, this study incorporates an existing detector, specifically using the MRCNN, as the primary means of detecting faces with various orientations. Moreover, a significant advantage of this method is its flexibility to incorporate various 3D models, including those with multiple landmarks, which enables it to handle complex shapes more effectively. Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the history and development of bond-based Peridynamics, examining various extensions of the theory while also exploring potential avenues for enhancing PD models to address pressing issues in computational mechanics. A bond-based PD framework for fluid-dynamics is introduced, along with numerical results demonstrating the method's efficacy, before concluding with recommendations for future research within this field. A new concept for bond-based PD models is proposed, along with a numerical implementation for nonlinear elasticity problems. This includes a non-local extension of the J2 elastoplasticity model, which is also subjected to numerical testing, providing insights into the behavior of bond-based PD models in nonlinear applications. Due to its clarity and thorough exploration of bond-based Peridynamics, this work is an essential reference for anyone looking to understand and utilize PD models in computational mechanics. A significant contribution of this study revolves around the rehabilitation of bond-based PD models as a coherent and systematic approach to modeling real-world phenomena, rather than an ad-hoc numerical method. This, coupled with the presentation of a comprehensive history of PD theories in chapter 2, has paved the way for revisiting and re-evaluating the foundations of computational mechanics with a non-local perspective. This study provides a valuable insight that can be applied to other areas of computational mechanics, where the impact of non-locality on material behavior needs to be modeled accurately. One such area is fracture mechanics, where the extension of PD models to tackle the emergence of new surfaces requires careful consideration of non-local effects. This study has ignited a renewed interest in bond-based PD models among researchers in the field of computational mechanics, leading to a surge in new research and collaborations. This has resulted in a proliferation of new PD models and implementations being proposed, which are now being utilized to model complex fracture patterns and material failures with unprecedented levels of accuracy. This, in turn, has enabled the accurate simulation of damage evolution and fracture in various applications, ranging from the study of concrete fracture to the simulation of material failure in metal forming processes. Numerous applications in chemistry and materials science rely heavily on modeling systems with multiple interacting particles. A crucial challenge in this context involves efficiently exploring configurational space, especially when dealing with complex systems that can't be solved analytically. Despite its widespread use, the thermostat control method known as the velocity verlet algorithm has some drawbacks, specifically when employed with a large step size for Langevin Dynamics simulations. This limitation stems from an inconsistent thermostat that causes systematic configurational bias, leading to impaired mixing and decreased precision in Monte Carlo moves. To address this issue, we present an alternative velocity verlet algorithm that maintains a consistent thermostat, thereby eliminating the systematic bias. This revised algorithm exhibits superior performance, mixing longer molecular trajectories with minimal thermal displacement. Our approach also facilitates the creation of move kernels that blend MC and MD configurations, leading to a significant reduction in the acceptance rate of MC moves. When put to the test on three distinct test cases – a harmonic oscillator, a Lennard-Jones fluid, and LAMMPs LAMMPS simulations LAMMPS simulations – this new algorithm outperforms the standard velocity verlet method, especially when using larger step sizes. The revised algorithm yields a substantial boost in efficiency, achieving a 5-130 times improvement, for both small and large step sizes. This new algorithm represents a major breakthrough, capable of handling complex molecular dynamics simulations with a large number of particles, providing a more practical path to achieving greater speed and efficiency. As a result, we anticipate this new algorithm will become a go-to method for solving a wide range of chemical and materials science problems. With its enhanced performance, it is especially well-suited for being an automatic choice in combined MC/MD protocols, which will be given the codename CMV. Source code for this project is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexsolisg/cmvm. In addition, we have formulated an open challenge to measure the performance of this algorithm against other variants of the velocity verlet algorithm, which can be executed using a publicly available benchmark developed from the LAMMPS code. This benchmark, known as CMV-Bench, is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexsolisg/cmvm-bench, and is an easy way for researchers to evaluate the performance of this algorithm against other variants. This project seeks to investigate whether such models, specifically the Schwarzschild metric, are compatible with the highly complex conditions seen in binary black hole mergers. This study uses a combination of numerical relativity and direct integration methods to model binary black hole mergers in an environment of waving particles. The focus is on analyzing how these waving particles impact gravitational waves through various frequencies, structures, and characteristics, and whether such effects can be captured by a simple model that considers the impact of these particles on the merger. Ultimately, this project aims to provide a framework for developing more accurate initial conditions for numerical relativity simulations, allowing them to account for the complex conditions seen in binary black hole mergers. This, in turn, could lead to more accurate predictions of merger rates based on observations of gravitational waves. Researchers utilized a novel sonic lens material called poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) for enhanced photoacoustic tomography. Unlike traditional sonic lens materials, PLGA maintains its low acoustic impedance difference with skin, approximately 1.7-2 MRayls, even after being implanted in the skin for several days. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("surface seal") either based on impact velocity or sphere size have yielded mixed results, showing significant variation depending on the specific sphere used. To gain a more detailed understanding, researchers studied the 0.0495 to 0.0987 m diameter sphere range at velocities from 0.26 to 3.8 m/s. They employed high-speed cameras to analyze multiple spheres at each of 36 unique velocity-sphere size combinations. Their research revealed a complex, nonlinear relationship between sphere size and the surface seal phenomenon, influenced by both the formation of air bubbles and the flow of water. To model this interaction, they developed a new "normal impact depth" (NID) to provide a unified framework for understanding surface seal, encompassing both the shallow water regime and the splash dome closure regime. Their model accurately predicted the time it takes for the splash dome to close in all 36 tested scenarios. NID offers a clear, easily visualized understanding of the surface seal process, showing how the depth of the initial water layer affects the time it takes for the sphere to seal with the water's surface. Building upon this knowledge, they propose adjusting the water entry load to a more intuitive "normal impact load" (NIL), which takes into account the specific pressure at the point of impact. This new load framework highlights the intricate relationship between surface seal and normal impact load, demonstrating how a particular sphere size may exhibit optimal surface seal performance at a certain velocity due to an optimal balance of factors including flow turbulence, water layer thickness, and the sphere's ability to displace water. To further validate their model, they conducted additional tests to analyze and model the time it takes for the sphere to seal over a wider range of normal impact depths, collecting a total of 270 new data points. These results demonstrate how the water entry surface seal performance of spheres can be optimized by selecting a sphere size that strikes a balance between its volume and surface area. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the water entry surface seal phenomenon, encompassing both the scientific principles underlying it and the development of a new model that predicts its behavior. We uncover an unresolvable dilemma arising from the choice-less box game, a variant of the famous box game experiment designed to illustrate the paradoxical consequences of selecting variables that influence outcomes. As the issue stands, no consensus exists regarding how the experiment's results should be interpreted. Our analysis aims to present an integral explanation of the problem by exploring its fundamental properties and the underlying frameworks it involves. Furthermore, we outline several experimental prototypes that could provide a path towards resolving the debate. These prototypes leverage the choice-less box game to investigate the complex relationship between choice, reality, and consistency, employing the robust framework of modal epistemic logic to achieve this understanding. Ultimately, our work demonstrates that even the most straightforward versions of the choice-less box game can give rise to paradoxical situations, challenging our current comprehension of the experimental design. As a result, we emphasize the importance of experimental research in validating theoretical frameworks and the critical role that simplicity should play in the design of box game experiments. Additionally, we explore the connection between the choice-less box game paradox and other fundamental issues in physics, while also considering the ethical implications of conducting the experiment. With regard to the experimental design, we advocate for a flexible approach that adapts the protocol based on the specific circumstances, utilizing the concept of an 'epistemic protocol' that captures this idea. Furthermore, we introduce a novel notion of 'consistent implementation,' along with a corresponding modal-epistemic-implementation logic, to better evaluate the results obtained from the experiment. With this enhanced analysis, we are better equipped to handle more complex variants of the choice-less box game, such as those involving multiple players or alternative decision-making processes. As we push the boundaries of this research further, we are confident that it will continue to illuminate the intricate relationship between choice, reality, and consistency, while also inspiring new scientific experiments and theoretical breakthroughs. With regard to the experimental procedure, we emphasize the significance of controlling the 'implementation baseline,' acknowledging that this experiment has the potential to significantly impact our current understanding of the choice-less box game paradox. With our work, we have demonstrated that even the simplest versions of the choice-less box game can give rise to paradoxical situations, while also showing that the best outcome for this experiment would be one that either confirms our current understanding or provides a clear alternative. With our analysis, we have provided a framework that can be applied to evaluate the results obtained from the experiment, along with a new perspective on the choice-less box game that highlights its fundamental connection to the paradoxical consequences of selecting variables

As a result, this method has the capability to generate specific chemical structures, such as chemical compounds and polymers with the functional groups of certain proteins. The new framework, including the polymer design method, has its parameters available online at the CodeOcean repository coded https://codeocean.io/v/2b56nd. Through an example of designing polymers that can interact with lysozyme, the new method demonstrates its effectiveness. Additionally, an extension of the framework that incorporates a score function for compounds has been introduced, and it has been applied to create compounds with the functional groups of the p53 protein. This new method could potentially be useful for predicting properties of chemical compounds and polymers, based on their structure, and may help identify potential applications of certain compounds. The new framework, including the polymer design method, has been named the Graph-IPNeural system. Due to limitations in available resources, medical professionals are often forced to ventilate multiple patients on the same machine, known as multi-patient ventilation (MPV). Although this practice has been employed since the 1980s, particularly in pediatric settings, MPV remains a contentious topic that requires further study, especially in critical care settings affected by pandemics. The issue is to determine how to optimize ventilator settings for one patient without negatively impacting the health of the other. By framing this issue as a multi-objective optimization problem that incorporates constraints, we aim to illustrate the process of solving such a problem using direct transcription for its non-differentiable form. A case study is presented to demonstrate this approach on a specific ventilator model, with its control system designed to regulate the airflow for one patient while minimizing the risk of lung injury in the other. Due to the large number of decision variables and constrained interactions between the patients' respiratory dynamics, this problem poses significant computational challenges. A key aspect of our strategy is the conversion of the multi-objective problem into a single objective problem by weighting the individual objectives, with this weighting determined through an initial set of high-resolution simulations. Identifying tumors in the esophagus via CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To improve the accuracy of automatic tumor detection, a new, densely-focused dense neural network design called the Dilated Dense Focus Dense Unet (DDDAUnet) has been created. This innovative network, centered on dense connections that concentrate on key areas within slices and focus layers that capture detailed information from narrowed-down regions, outperformed existing CT-based segmentation approaches like Contour-based methods, Region-based models, and popular neural network architectures like UNets and DenseUnets in multiple benchmark tests. A dataset comprised of low-contrast abdominal scans from 50 different patients, obtained from two sources with varying image qualities, was utilized for training and evaluating the new network. The implementation of a highly-effective tumor candidate selection algorithm, prioritizing efficiency and ease of use, significantly boosted the DDDAUnet's performance. The outstanding results achieved by the DDDAUnet, coupled with its exceptional practical applications, suggests that this network has great potential for realizing effective tumor segmentation in real-world applications. The source code of the DDDAUnet has been made available for public use. To further enhance the accuracy of tumor segmentation, a new methodology called the Dense Focus Context layer was introduced, considering factors like context information and spatial correlations. This innovative approach outperformed the DDDAUnet in multiple experiments, indicating its superiority. The new method's source code has also been made available for public use. The challenging task of esophageal tumor segmentation in CT images has been successfully overcome by the DDDAUnet, yielding outstanding quantitative and qualitative results. To achieve this, a high-quality dataset consisting of 50 different patients was created, and further developed into a part of the Low-Dose CT segmentation challenge. The DDDAUnet's exceptional performance in tumor segmentation has enabled the exploration of additional medical applications, such as the detection of cancers in the heart, lungs, and liver. The relatively small size of the DDDAUnet, along with its fast processing times, makes it suitable for deployment on mobile devices, thereby opening up new possibilities for the diagnosis of diseases in clinical settings. The examination of the DDDAUnet's performance in low-light conditions has led to the discovery of its remarkable ability to overcome this challenge, resulting in the demonstration of its capabilities in the Low-Dose CT segmentation challenge

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering decisions during the drilling process. We propose a data-driven approach that utilizes ensemble methods for uncertainty quantification to guide such decisions in real-time, based on the results from analytical and numerical models. We utilize well logs from multiple wells to build a static reservoir model, which informs the development of a dynamic model that predicts fluid levels during the drilling process. It also serves as the basis for identifying potential wells and assessing their feasibility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a representative offshore sand reservoir. The method involves utilizing an advanced radial model that mimics the behavior of a finite layer during drilling, based on which we generate ensembles to forecast fluid levels during drilling. The association between well placement and drilling costs is modeled using a DISC function, which facilitates potential well identification. The proposed technique provides accurate predictions of fluid levels, potential well paths, and drilling costs along with uncertainty quantification. It also compares predicted costs with actual costs from the study area, which demonstrates its usefulness. The proposed approach provides drilling supervisors with reliable, data-driven guidance to make informed decisions during real-time geosteering. It also facilitates the assessment of risk associated with different well placement strategies, which can be utilized to optimize drilling operations. The proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to various reservoir models and potential well placement strategies. It can also be integrated with different forecasting models that predict fluid levels during drilling. The method's potential for upgrading to a dynamic model that considers interactions between reservoir layers during drilling is an area of potential development. It can be in the form of more sophisticated numerical models such as the CMG's ECLIPSE model. The proposed approach provides an optimal solution for upgrading to such models, which would provide even more accurate predictions of fluid levels during drilling. It can also integrate various potential well placement strategies, which can be defined through defined functions that can be utilized with the proposed DISC function. The proposed approach's potential for upgrading to such models, along with its ability to integrate various potential well placement strategies, makes it an ideal solution for the oil and gas industry. It can provide even more accurate predictions of fluid levels during drilling and even more feasible potential well paths, which can result in even more optimal well placement and even more cost savings. The proposed approach can also integrate various logging data, which can enhance its performance and provide even more accurate predictions of fluid levels during drilling

Named entity recognition (NER) is a core task in natural language processing and a key step in extracting entities from text for subsequent tasks like link extraction and information verification. Standard NER models typically rely on linear chain models and are often based on the sequence labelling hypothesis, but these approaches have limitations when dealing with nested entities. To overcome this, we propose using a second pass correction method to tackle this issue, but this introduces a label ambiguity problem that reduces NER's role to a partial task. To fully utilise NER's potential, we suggest reformulating nested NER as a whole-task parsing activity, eliminating the need for a separate resolution process. By doing so, we aim to investigate whether non-linear models can handle nested entities more effectively than their linear model counterparts. Our experiments show that when allowing for non-linearity, fully joint models outperform those constrained to linear chains by a significant margin, proving that the proposed approach is superior to the traditional sequence labelling framework for nested NER. Moreover, our results indicate that when non-linearity is factored in, the distinction between joint and individual models disappears, confirming that we have resolved the label ambiguity issue that plagues sequence labelling. Moreover, our analysis paves the way for further exploration of how to extend this successful approach to other natural language processing tasks that rely on NER, such as text classification and semantic role labelling, by demonstrating that the proposed NER model's superiority holds when these tasks are redefined as whole-task parsing activities. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/NRL/tree/master/Nested_NER, along with our model's configuration, which has been fully integrated into the standard NER evaluation toolkit, CoNLL2003, along with two additional evaluation metrics, to facilitate easy comparison with state-of-the-art NER models. Moreover, our results highlight the necessity to revisit and revise the standard sequence labelling benchmark for NER, by demonstrating that when allowed to do so, non-linear models outperform linear models by a substantial margin on the CoNLL2003 test set. Our analysis further indicates that when allowed to do so, models for the CoNLL2009 NER task, which feature fewer looser OOV definitions than those for the CoNLL2003 task, result in a lower score than those for the CoNLL2003 task, confirming that the issue with linear models is not solely due to OOVs. This research paper addresses the challenge of precise device location determination within a wireless sensor network, particularly one that uses the 802.15.4 protocol and is subject to interference between different technologies. To tackle this issue, a new algorithm called the Cross Technology Interference Location Algorithm (CTILA) has been developed to calculate a device's position by utilizing measurements of radio signal strength, along with a new metric called the Interference Free Distance. The CTILA algorithm is capable of operating in networks that suffer from cross technology interference, which significantly differs from existing location determination methods. A network simulator called OMNeT++, was utilized to evaluate the CTILA algorithm and compare its results to a reference scenario with no interference, revealing a trade-off between location accuracy and interference level. The study also investigated how different parameters such as network density, device speed, and scan interval affect the algorithm's performance, providing insight into the optimal selection of these parameters for the best location accuracy. The research findings provide a solid foundation for the implementation of the CTILA algorithm in real-world applications. To facilitate replication of the study, the developed code is freely available for download. The investigation explored two use cases - an indoor setting and a parking lot scenario - with the CTILA algorithm proving suitable for parking lot applications but requiring modification for indoor locations due to the greater impact of cross technology interference in enclosed spaces. The project's code is an open-source contribution to the ONET++ simulator. The study has been presented at notable conferences such as the IEEE ICC 2015 and the IEEE ICC 2016, with an extended version published as a research article in the journal Ad Hoc Networks. The project has received funding from the European Union's Seventh Framework Programme. The study has been carried out in collaboration with members of the ERTICO-SAfe and the University of Oulu. The project has been recognized with an award at the University of Oulu. The investigation has been conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the ethical guidelines for research, with the requirements for confidentiality and data security fulfilled by utilizing pseudonymized data and encrypting all communication. The study has been carried out within the framework of a formal research collaboration, with all parties signed to a collaborative agreement. The investigation has been overseen by a dedicated steering committee with clear objectives and milestones. The study has been conducted in accordance with the established protocols and procedures, with the results verified by a third-party expert. The investigation has provided a clear answer to the research question, with the findings validated by multiple techniques.

While Code-Mixed Language Planning is implemented in highly effective manner in several countries, a significant obstacle hindering its execution is the scarcity of advanced NLP technology capable of managing code-mixed texts. This paper to some extent bridges this knowledge gap by providing HelsinkiNLP challenges confronting NLP developers when working with code-mixed data, specifically emanating from India and Finland. It also delves into various codemerging patterns encountered in datasets from these regions and highlights the scarcity of resources available for the Indian context. Finally, it presents Part-of-Speech and Dependency Parsing benchmarks designed to assess current NLP models' performance on code-mixed data and underscores the necessity for more comprehensive tests covering additional languages and NLP tasks. This research is an initiative by the HelsinkiNLP group to contribute positively to the development of code-mixed NLP with expertise applicable to Multilingual societies. It is hoped that through disseminating this study at prominent NLP conferences like the Conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the International Conference on Learning Representations, it will attract top NLP researchers to participate and advance the field. This knowledge is intended to benefit not just India and Finland but any Multilingual society where English and local languages intersect. From a methodological point of view, this study is a social experiment that introduces the HelsinkiNLP Code-Mixed Challenges and Benchmarks to the NLP community and observes how the field responds to these issues. It is worth noting that primary data collected for this research comprises NLP tasks executed by publicly available machine learning models, whereas secondary data incorporates existing research on code-mixed NLP examined in this study. This research is an attempt to provide knowledge useful to the NLP community, NLP4All, and in particular, the Code-Mixed NLP branch of this domain. It is also a demonstration of how the impact of prior research can be evaluated and the knowledge of the NLP community validated through the high-level theme of state-of-the-art analysis followed by a social experiment. This knowledge is beneficial not just to the code-mixed NLP community but to the broader NLP4All community as well. It is hoped that this study will attract top NLP researchers to participate and advance the field, thereby contributing positively to the development of code-mixed NLP with expertise applicable to Multilingual societies. It is also hoped that through disseminating this study at prominent NLP conferences like the Conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the International Conference on Learning Representations, it will attract further attention from the NLP community

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the exception of taodite (Ta$_2$O$_5$), have been extensively studied, yet taodite itself remains poorly understood.  To gain insight into its behavior, we compared multiple ab-initio methods including GGA and GGA+U to Monte Carlo simulations to determine the fundamental lattice structure of taodite.  Our results indicate that, contrary to previous research, taodite exhibits a non-stoichiometric lattice, with oxygen atoms occupying two distinct positions and we further found that GGA+U method provides the most accurate predictions for this specific compound.  Our data also suggest that GGA method overestimates the cell volume by approximately 10%, while GGA+U method yields a much more precise estimate of around 1%.  Our taodite model, derived from the GGA+U method, displays the same electric field distribution as observed in x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, providing further confirmation of our results.  To validate our findings, we calculated the specific heat capacity of taodite using both ab-initio methods and experimental data, and our outcomes show a close correlation, further supporting our taodite model.  Lastly, we investigated how oxygen vacancies affect the electric field distribution in taodite and our results indicate that vacancies have a negligible impact and so another study, that found the creation of oxygen vacancies at room temperature to be highly improbable, is validated.  To conclude, our research uncovers the fundamental lattice structure of taodite with a focus on its oxygen vacancy content, confirming that it does not incorporate vacancies, which contrasts with another study indicating it may have some.  Furthermore, our outcomes suggest that GGA+U method yields the most accurate results for this specific compound, producing a model that accurately replicates experimental data, specifically x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and specific heat capacity results.  This model can serve as a reference point for other researchers working with taodite.  Lastly, our research introduces a new discussion about the effect of oxygen vacancies in taodite, albeit with just one study in agreement, which demands further scientific investigation to be confirmed.  As a result, we propose that experimental researchers, working with taodite, take note of our taodite model and incorporate it into their oxygen vacancy creation processes.  On the other hand, theoretical researchers are encouraged to contribute in confirming our results by reproducing our data and developing new pathways to validate our model, specifically regarding oxygen vacancies, which is just one study

An analysis of users sharing misinformation on Reddit across the United States was conducted to examine how the pattern of misinformation dissemination changed with time, particularly in the context of the Big Shift - a significant and longstanding migration trend in the US. Researchers used a dataset consisting of nearly 700 million comments made by Reddit users in the US over a 7-year period, starting from 2017. To identify users who repeatedly shared misinformation, a machine learning model was used to classify a subset of Reddit users as either frequent spreaders or non-frequent spreaders. It was observed that areas with net domestic out-migration exhibited higher rates of user-generated misinformation compared to areas with net migration. Moreover, analyses using both county and user-level data showed that the association between geographic regions and misinformation dissemination held true, reducing the impact of individual factors such as education, income, and urban-rural location. To explore potential reasons for this phenomenon, the researchers examined demographic changes, population size, education levels, and economic conditions in the regions, but surprisingly found no significant correlations with the observed patterns. To further validate the findings, the researchers leveraged an independent dataset from the NewsCorp Fact Checking dataset, confirming that the observed patterns of misinformation dissemination were consistent with fact-checking data. Humanitarian organizations, refugees, and asylum seekers frequently turn to Contact Forms on non-governmental organization websites for help. Unfortunately, website owners are often targeted by scammers who utilize these contact forms to deceive individuals and create unwanted situation. Presently, there is a lack of effective method to identify and block these unwanted submissions. To address this challenge, we propose a novel mathematical approach, along with a practical system incorporating machine learning techniques, to detect suspicious incidents in fast information flows. Experiments using real-world data from the website of a prominent humanitarian organization reveal that our system is capable of identifying a high percentage of known scammers and maintains excellent performance even with a limited training dataset. Furthermore, a key advantage of our system is its ability to provide website owners with clear, easy-to-understand reasons for suspected spam submissions, thereby reducing reliance on black-box machine learning methods. The system we developed is currently available online at the website of the mentioned humanitarian organization. It is also open-source and available for download on GitHub, under the Apache License, allowing other website owners to replicate its effectiveness. By implementing this system, website owners can significantly reduce the burden of manually reviewing unwanted submissions, minimizing delays in responding to genuine requests for help. Additionally, this system contributes a significant step towards developing an automatic system that can block unwanted submissions, thereby protecting website owners from spam and junk. Teaching robots through demonstration relies heavily on audio feedback from humans, yet the inherent difficulties of processing speech and observing actions complicate this process. To overcome these challenges, researchers demonstrate the necessity of analyzing the sound produced during demonstration, as well as action sequences. This paper delves into the complex interrelation between speech and action in human teaching by investigating the varied acoustic structures used by humans to explain, demonstrate, and combine manipulation tasks. Our data shows significant differences in speech patterns based on task similarity and the relationship between speech and action, indicating that certain speech is closely tied to specific actions. Our findings also reveal that human teachers often use a combination of describing actions through sound and providing detailed explanations, leading to a greater understanding of how humans communicate through demonstration. Our study's results can be utilized to create more efficient speech-action based teaching methods, while its implications may also be applied to other human communication methods, such as text-based instruction of robot tasks. Our study's data and experiments are publicly available for reproducibility purposes. To improve robot learning through demonstration, researchers should consider the complex acoustic structures involved in human teaching, and therefore, we suggest the term "acoustic-practical action sequence" to better capture the human teaching of robot actions via speech. By incorporating this complex speech structure, we may enhance robot performance when taught through demonstration. Our initial evaluation indicates that describing the acoustic structure of demonstration speech before showing the action results in a 23% decrease in error rate and a 25% decrease in action sequence complexity when teaching a new task. A connected subtree with the specified properties can be obtained by applying the algorithm to a subset of the original node set. Furthermore, this algorithm facilitates the development of a method for assigning identities to nodes in a connected tree. As a result, it enables the creation of a connected binary tree with randomly generated left and right child relationships between nodes. The algorithm also allows for the derivation of a procedure to randomly generate a connected forest, effectively achieving the same outcome as the N-ary random connection algorithm proposed by Knuth. The algorithm's properties, including its performance, are examined and its potential applications explored. Recent advances in neural machine translation are largely based on large corpus-trained models with little consideration for pre-existing dictionaries. This study suggests incorporating a monolingual lexicon database into neural machine translation models, which can facilitate translation and reduce the requirement for parallel corpora in model training. Experiments revealed that introducing a lexicon database with a substantial number of entries (around 10,000) does not necessarily result in the best performance. Instead, a smaller set of carefully selected words with high frequency and less noise led to the most significant improvement in translation accuracy. We also explored different lexicon database sizes and found that word embedding-based methods can effectively handle large vocabularies, whereas character-based models perform best on words with no clear visual representation. Our proposed approach achieved a notable increase in translation accuracy on English-French and English-German test sets, outperforming the strong baseline system by a 0.8-1.4 char-error rate. The improved models, along with the lexicon database and source code, are available for download. Leveraging a monolingual lexicon database offers a promising pathway to enhancing neural machine translation performance. Our work provides a foundation for exploring other types of knowledge databases that could complement neural translation systems. There are numerous potential knowledge databases with various formats that could be integrated into neural machine translation models, enabling them to access a wide range of knowledge and substantially boost the accuracy and diversity of translations. Furthermore, this type of model can facilitate bidirectional translation and help eliminate any introduced errors during the incorporation of the lexicon database. Our future research focuses on integrating multiple knowledge databases, exploring different learning methods, and combining neural machine translation models with other models, such as sequence-to-sequence models without attention, to reveal the full capabilities of neural machine translation systems. Despite the critical nature of this task, few studies have attempted to automate non-invasive quality assessments that ensure patient comfort and accurate research findings. We address this issue by developing an innovative, fully-automated approach called BQA-net, which utilizes deep learning to detect substandard MRI data across various scanner platforms. By combining multi-modal MRI data with easily obtainable patient information, we've created a versatile model that efficiently identifies poor-quality scans on a batch level. However, their distant counterparts have a significant issue - they are obscured by the universe's lensing effect, making their actual brightness appear different from their true brightness. This study uses the Pantheon SN dataset, along with the DESv4 weak lensing power spectrum, to calculate the impact of this lensing effect on the estimation of the universe's cosmic expansion. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity noise masks the signals. This study employs least-squares deconvolution with various line lists to minimize activity-induced variability and enhance the detection of planets. Our analysis utilizes both a systematic approach with a parametric model and a randomised model to select line lists. The results show that the former yields better outcomes, likely because it is more effective at identifying line lists that are uncorrelated with stellar activity. The best line lists selected by both methods exhibit minimal variability and are composed of lines spanning a broad range of wavelengths. These lines are also the least active in the chromosphere, as evidenced by their low flux compared to the entire spectral range. The analysis suggests that the most effective line lists for detecting planets are those including the strongest lines, specifically those with the highest continuum and lowest chromospheric flux. The use of these line lists through least-squares deconvolution can significantly reduce the residual flux variability by approximately 50%. This approach offers a valuable strategy for reducing stellar activity noise when detecting exoplanets, allowing the identification of planets even in highly active stellar systems. The most suitable line lists can also provide valuable information about the stellar activity levels. The employed analysis and the line lists identified in this study can be applied to a range of stars, extending from the most commonly observed G stars to M dwarfs. The development of this strategy contributes to the improvement of planet detection, especially in highly active stellar systems, and paves the way for the use of line lists as an indicator of a star's activity levels. Furthermore, this study highlights the potential for least-squares deconvolution to detect planets in data sets where the planet signal falls below the detection threshold. This paper presents a new approach to entity recommendations using Wikipedia's interconnected structure. Unlike other approaches that rely on user interactions or ratings, our method leverages Wikipedia's category system to create a layered graph representation, facilitating efficient entity recommendations. By combining Wikipedia's category relationships with knowledge graph information, we develop a novel paradigm for entity recommendations, characterized by (1) recommendations aligned with Wikipedia's category hierarchy and (2) considerations of both user preferences and the structure of Wikipedia's categories. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we conduct an experiment to demonstrate users' satisfaction with recommendations generated using our method, indicating a clear preference for predictions that adhere to Wikipedia's category hierarchy over random predictions. Furthermore, our approach yields recommendations with a higher level of diversity and relevance compared to established recommendation methods. We make available a Wikipedia-specific entity recommendation framework, alongside category-specific recommendation results for English language Wikipedia users. Additionally, we provide English language Wikipedia category maps corresponding to our model's parameter settings. These resources can be utilized to develop a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation application, capable of providing users with tailored suggestions to explore and engage with Wikipedia's vast content repository. By integrating our recommendation framework with Wikipedia's Mobile View, we create an accessible and user-friendly interface for users to interact with Wikipedia's category system, receiving accurate and diverse entity recommendations in return. This combined approach, comprising Wikipedia's layered graph structure and our entity recommendation model, can be described as a WikiRec system. The knowledge we gather from Wikipedia's category system and our recommendation model, collectively known as WikiRec-data, raises interesting research inquiries regarding knowledge acquisition, model development, and user studies within the Wikipedia ecosystem. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the standard Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold. Building upon this, we also prove that a trivial steady Cotton soliton occurs under the condition that the Reeb vector field's eigenvalue of the Ricci operator is non-negative. Moreover, we prove that a shrinkage-type Cotton soliton cannot exist on nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Finally, we demonstrate the incompatibility of a conformal Killing vector field with an eigenvalue of the Ricci operator on these manifolds. Based on the above findings, we establish that a non-trivial steady Cotton soliton with an incompressible distribution can not exist on nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Building upon these results, we generalize and prove analogous theorems for a type of vector field, specifically an operator-related vector field, which leads to a vector field-related soliton. This generalized proof relies on an algebraic approach rather than an explicit calculation of the Schouten-Nijenhuis bracket. Consequently, our findings provide further insight into nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds, contributing to a broader understanding of these manifolds' geometry. To achieve success in more complex discussions, models need to navigate through numerous statements and steer clear of irrelevant topics. To address this issue, we've developed the MultiTalk dataset, which incorporates an exceptionally elaborate tree structure to mimic sophisticated conversations. This dataset incorporates 15,000 text samples divided among 9 topics and features a vast array of branching paths - up to 27 conversation stages from a single initial statement. Our evaluation indicates that the next statement in a conversation is often the least reliable indicator of the next successive statement. By comparing different models' performance, we've identified that transforming input statements into a set of coherent groups through clustering significantly improves a model's ability to predict future statements. Our ultimate evaluation standard, combines various metrics including sub-tree accuracy, 1-step to 10-step prediction accuracy, and diverse evaluation branches, to assess a model's overall conversational understanding. To facilitate seamless comparison between different models, we've introduced the MultiTalk Evaluation Toolkit, an open-source, highly customizable evaluation framework. Our primary evaluation of this framework involves testing five different models, and our results show that while they excel in certain aspects, none have mastered the art of predicting future conversational dialogue with certainty. By overcoming present shortcomings and developing a more comprehensive evaluation framework, we're one step closer to creating gold-standard data that can reliably assess a model's conversational understanding, especially its ability to engage in complex discussions. Our ultimate goal is to integrate this evaluation framework into ongoing conversation datasets to refine models that can excel in deeply branched conversations. By doing so, we aim to pave the way for future Conversation Evaluation Boards to establish universally accepted standards for evaluating the quality of conversational models. Our code, along with the MultiTalk dataset and evaluation toolkit, is now openly available for the community to explore and build upon. Our statistical approach, known as MAPLE, assessed the association between these genomic features and the traits in question by considering multiple feature types simultaneously. Our analysis revealed significant associations between genomic features and the traits for at least one gene in 14 out of 18 traits examined. Notably, we found little evidence that our results are biased towards regions of the genome that have been well-studied in the past. Our study is part of a larger initiative that enables the exploration of genome-wide association data for any given set of genes, traits or genomic regions of interest. This study specifically examined 18 traits identified as being associated with an increased risk of disease in individuals with certain occupations, based on data from GENOME-WIDE ASSOCIATION STUDIES and the GENOMIC ENHANCEMENT BROWSER. $\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: they serve as lecture notes for a 4-hour mini-course on $\tau$-tilting theory presented at the 2019 Conference on Representation Theory in Shanghai, and they also provide an overview of the development of $\tau$-tilting theory to date. Building on the foundation established by Bautista and Hernandez in their 2016 University of Iowa notes, we have incorporated an additional key area of research into the content -- specifically, the relationship between $\tau$-tilting modules and Bautista-Hernandez $\tau$-functors. It is our hope that these notes will be beneficial to both the expert and the novice $\tau$-tilting theorist. As such, we have included a brief introduction to the underlying background from the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, and we have also included a novel proof of the fact that $\tau$-functors preserve $\tau$-tilting modules -- a result that implies the equivalences of the category of $\tau$-tilting modules to the category of $\tau$-tilting modules obtained through $\tau$-functors defined by Bautista and Hernandez. Additionally, we have a new result regarding the structure of $\tau$-tilting modules in the case where the algebra has a single non-deterministic simple module -- this involves the use of a Bass series to determine the Bautista-Hernandez $\tau$-length of a module. Current neural conversational dialogue models rely on neural network architectures similar to those used for classification tasks, such as transformer-based languages models to engage in dialogue. While successful, it has been observed that these models frequently struggle to understand the context and maintain a coherent semantic structure in conversations. One factor contributing to this difficulty is the vast semantic variety encountered in conversations, which exceeds that of NLI tasks. To better comprehend the rise of sophisticated semantic variations in conversations and the implications for model performance, this study introduces a new paradigm that emphasizes semantic diversity. It challenges models to anticipate the next utterance in a conversation, considering the entire dialogue history and the diversity of all possible responses. A large-scale dataset, diverse to exceed that of NLI, has been created for three distinct topics to support this challenge. It was found that selecting the most diverse descriptor for a conversation, as opposed to a single central description, significantly boosts the performance of models, especially when they are forced to consider the entire dialogue history. It was further discovered that advanced architectures, although exceling in classification tasks, sometimes fail in conversational settings. Ultimately, this study suggests that two key factors govern semantic variety in conversations: the diverse selection of descriptions and the intricate context provided by each new utterance. To tackle these factors, a novel simple architecture called the Diversity Context Model was proposed, which combines local and global context through two descriptors, successfully outperforming all existing models. The models examined in this study have been trained and tested in an open-source code available for public use. It is hoped that this work will contribute to the advancement of sophisticated semantic structures in conversations. Building on the development of self-driving cars, this research focuses on identifying hazardous actions by leading vehicles from a dataset of lane change video sequences. It integrates a unique approach that involves generating segmentation masks to recognize the presence, orientation, and movement of the leading vehicle's rear. By utilizing a deep spatiotemporal neural network, it accurately predicts whether the leading vehicle's rear indicates the need to change lanes, turn left or right, or move sideways. Notably, this approach for model training includes a innovative transfer learning method called Segmentation Mask Transfer, where a leading vehicle with a complex shape is substituted with a simple shape, thereby reducing overfitting. This innovative approach results in a significant improvement in performance, achieving an overall accuracy of 84.5%, in comparison to 78.6% achieved by a baseline model, and 81.6% achieved by another deep learning model, on a specially designed evaluation tool called the Hazard Action Dataset Evaluator (HADE). Furthermore, this research demonstrates the superiority of its algorithm over multiple baseline models, indicating its potential for real-world application. Additionally, it highlights the necessity for a more robust training method, due to the limited size of its dataset, amounting to only 2000 samples, in comparison to datasets containing 5000 to 50000 samples. This paper presents an efficient way to prepare data for training, as well as a pioneering approach for identifying the leading vehicle's rear, orientation, and movement, in comparison to methods relying on the detection of the entire leading vehicle. It also presents HADE, a novel evaluation tool, along with its integration with ObamaBar, a recently introduced tool. This paper is a revised and expanded version of the initial study presented at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2019, incorporating feedback from multiple reviewers. It has been further updated to include additional analysis, along with more comprehensive experimental results, in addition to the inclusion of recent related work on action recognition, in order to provide a clear and comprehensive overview of the field. The rapid growth in data creation and the need for continuous model updating in scenarios with shifting classes and the arrival of new learning materials highlight the significance of incremental learning algorithms.  A key challenge in this field is dealing with class imbalances, where certain classes have significantly fewer instances than others.  This study investigates algorithms for learning incrementally in the presence of class imbalances and compares traditional techniques with a novel method specifically designed for this purpose.  Our proposed approach, which involves initially training the model using a balanced sample of the data and then updating it with a focus on the underrepresented class through weight adjustment, demonstrates superior performance.  Our research provides a comprehensive analysis of the performance enhancement achieved by this method, detailing the precise benefits it offers over conventional techniques.  We also explore the effect of different calibration methods on our unique approach, testing it on a recently introduced benchmark suite.  Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, confirming its superiority over benchmark algorithms in addressing the challenge of class imbalances in incremental learning.  Our implementation of the algorithm, along with detailed experiment results and code, is made available for others to build upon.  We anticipate this contribution to spur further exploration into the development of advanced algorithms capable of handling the complexities of real-world scenarios involving class imbalances and the arrival of new data.  To this end, we introduce the concept of incremental learning as a sequence of independent trials, with each update representing a standalone test of the model's performance, with the aim of facilitating straightforward evaluation of future algorithms. Recent advancements in wide-ranging computing tasks like Cloud, Artificial Intelligence, and Virtualization have driven the demand for Data Centers to process multiple workloads simultaneously. As a result, modern Data Centers employ a variety of techniques, such as cache partitioning, to achieve high throughput while minimizing power consumption. However, the increasing complexity of digital circuits in modern computing systems has made it challenging to achieve reliable operation within the decreasing voltage margins available to them. This research presents HyperDegrade, a novel technology that integrates the complexities of today's sophisticated digital circuits into its design. By incorporating a failure-aware voltage management system that recognizes digital errors resulting from voltage reduction as a circuit degradation, HyperDegrade rewards creators of stable circuits with lower production costs and enhanced market appeal. In contrast to previous methods that focus on throughput and leverage system-level redundancy, HyperDegrade introduces a new design criterion called "degradability" to the chip design process. Through the implementation of a binary search-based voltage tuning algorithm that determines optimal voltage reductions for a given workload, HyperDegrade achieves significant power reductions while ensuring the reliability of computing systems. Experimental results show that HyperDegrade can cut power consumption by half or more, from GHz-level frequencies, in real-world applications like web servers, artificial intelligence, and database systems. The design has been tested using the CACTI and the OpenRISC processor models, indicating that it can integrate complex digital circuits like FLIGHT WEIGHT, VLSI, and BP/SP accelerators without compromising performance. Furthermore, the analysis of a range of cloud workloads using the Simics simulator has found that HyperDegrade can reduce power consumption by as much as 3.11 times, from GHz-level frequencies, in real computing systems. In addition, the design can also minimize thermal variations, achieving a 1.23 times decrease in temperature standard deviation. The implementation of HyperDegrade on a prototype OpenRISC processor has demonstrated its effectiveness, resulting in a 1.78 times decrease in power consumption and a 1.15 times decrease in temperature variation when running a range of cloud workloads. The research offers various integration strategies for HyperDegrade, including a simple module addition, a custom processor design, and a memory controller modification. To address the discrepancy in the muon's second generation anomaly, we examine a scenario in which the Higgs boson plays a crucial role by entering the loop calculation in the $O(10\,\text{GeV})$ energy range of the Anomaly-Effective Field Theory (aEFPT). To achieve this, we develop a contact interaction representation of the aEFPT, establishing a connection between the Higgs' mass and the energy scale of the theory. By comparing the Higgs' contribution with that of other particles, we identify the energy range in which the Higgs' impact is significant, and we explore the potential of the HIMS experiment to detect the Higgs' influence directly. Our analysis reveals that, to resolve the anomaly, the Higgs' contribution must interact with other phenomena, such as the emergence of the muon non-universality observed in the B-meson sector. The proposed B-factory experiments, Higgs-sensitive muon pair production searches at the Large Hadron Collider, and the MUSE experiment at the muon storage ring will significantly contribute to understanding the role of the Higgs in resolving the anomaly. The discrepancy can be addressed by introducing a small mass for the W-boson, however, this solution will be heavily constrained by forthcoming W-boson precision measurements. To find the optimal beam energy for the MUSE experiment, we examine the possible outcomes of varying the beam energy, energy scale, and W-boson mass in the loop calculation. Moreover, we outline the salient features of an expanded Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) that integrates the aEFPT and the Higgs' contribution, providing a unified theoretical framework that can be tested by both the particle and antiparticle experiments. The most pertinent signatures of the Higgs' involvement will be observable in the MUSE experiment, particularly at the proposed beam energy of 6 GeV. The detection of the Higgs' contribution will have far-reaching implications, enabling us to deduce the Higgs' interaction with the W-boson and the energy scale of the aEFPT, as well as accurately determine the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. The Higgs' role in resolving the anomaly will, in turn, provide insight into the underlying theory that addresses the discrepancy, thereby paving the way for developing a more comprehensive understanding of the fundamental laws governing the universe. Furthermore, we anticipate that the Higgs' involvement in the anomaly will significantly impact the interpretation of particle and antiparticle data in the B-meson

An novel approach is presented for determining the decay constant $C$ in the CKM matrix from a specific set of beauty meson decays involving photons, utilizing independent inputs for the photon energy and multiplicity. This method is utilized to derive $CF$ in two different ways, yielding results of $CF = 0.6104 \pm 0.0028 \pm 0.0018$ and $CF = 0.6105 \pm 0.0027 \pm 0.0017$, both of which are in line with the expected value based on $CF \approx \tan\theta_J$. The precision of these measurements, obtained with data amounts of $1$ and $2$ times $100$ pb^-$1$ respectively, indicates a potential for $CF$ determination with an uncertainty of less than $0.001$ in experiments using the LHCb setup at an 14 TeV proton-proton collision energy of $1$ times $10^{32}$ cm^-$2$. This new move enables us to separate twisted, tied, and stuck parts of a link, essentially mirroring the properties of a full twist. By incorporating this move, we can demonstrate that any two welded links are topologically equivalent if and only if they contain the same number of full twists. Moreover, this new move allows us to prove that any two classical links are topologically equivalent if and only if they contain the same number of full twists and/or crossings of a specific mirror-reflected form. In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CPU and GPU parallelization, has become essential. This study compares sequential (CPU) and distributed (GPU) approaches to matrix multiplication, considering factors like scalability, application, and potential gains. By illustrating a practical application and providing theoretical background, this research demonstrates the advantages of parallel processing using a matrix example from computer graphics, ultimately encouraging students to explore real-world examples combining computer science and mathematics. Furthermore, an associated project is offered for students to further explore matrix multiplication using a real-world case study. This research investigates the complex challenge of coordinating tasks among multiple agents within a network. In contrast to traditional approaches, these agents have restricted processing power and only brief time frames to make decisions. Furthermore, the simplicity of their state updates means that the system exhibits persistent synchronization across multiple tasks with minimal failure rates. Despite these conditions, the team has developed an uncomplicated, universal policy that enables them to successfully complete their tasks over any connected, well-structured network. The key feature of this achievement is the derivation of a specific parameter value for each agent, which is determined by a task-dependent computation and displayed in an agent-invariant form that does not require knowledge of the network structure. The simplicity of this approach is further illustrated by the fact that the best strategy for a given subproblem arises from the most straightforward possible solution method. We have been investigating the potential of amplitude-based resummation to achieve this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in predicting multiple observables with high precision, sometimes surpassing the precision achievable through grid-based resummation. However, we also encounter difficulties in validating our results, primarily stemming from the limited accuracy of sensitivity functions, which hinders our comparison with grid-based resummation. To move forward, we need to either improve the accuracy of sensitivity functions or alternatively derive a different cross-check for our precision predictions. Horizontal and vertical federated learning address different challenges in a decentralized machine learning context. While horizontal FL deals with models having similar data parameters but potentially different data, vertical FL is about models having the same data but potentially different features. As the majority of real-world applications fall into the vertical FL category, we decide to concentrate on it. Several attacks specifically designed for horizontal FL have been established, but our survey reveals that research on vertical FL attacks remains in its infancy. We aim to expand the existing body of knowledge on vertical FL attacks by exploring various categories of attacks, such as data manipulation, machine learning attacks, and cryptographic assaults. We also discuss the scope of modern machine learning models to be attacked, before which we provide a concise overview of the current state of vertical FL attacks for those who need it. One particular attack method that we explore in depth is the manipulation of data, which is exhibited through a new data manipulation attack we devised called 'Rectangular Masking Attack'. This new attack method varies from the widely known cluster-based manipulation attack in that it employs a mask with fewer categories than the model's classification does, which results in reduced accuracy for non-target users and better success for the attacker. We validate the effectiveness of this new attack by conducting multiple experiments using the PubMed-2000 dataset. Our results indicate that by adjusting the number of categories in the mask, the attacker is able to achieve a wide range of accuracy rates for the target model, which can be as low as 0.032 or as high as 0.898. Our study on vertical FL attacks also raises important issues regarding the evaluation of modern machine learning models, which we discuss through the context of this particular attack. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/RectangularMasking. We hope that our research on vertical FL attacks will inspire further exploration in this underdeveloped area and contribute to the development of more robust and secure vertical FL systems.
