In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. Furthermore, it fails to leverage the inherent structure within the data, resulting in poorly optimized kernels that can significantly impede the performance of kernel-based algorithms. This research presents an alternative approach to kernel approximation, centered on the concept of creating data-dependent random Fourier features, with the aim of enhancing both computational efficiency and overall performance. Through the development of a bespoke distortion-minimization algorithm, this approach yields optimized random features that not only match the computational efficiency of traditional methods but also exhibit a marked improvement in algorithmic precision, with notable results demonstrated across multiple benchmark datasets. Furthermore, this method holds a key advantage over Fourier Features, namely Fourier Features can not guarantee a uniform distribution over the projected data, whereas the proposed approach ensures a supply of uniform random features, thereby enabling the use of kernel-based algorithms in a wide range of applications requiring real-valued outputs. In our study, we developed a strategy to determine whether a group can be embedded into a wreath product. This method is based on the Cartesian decomposition concept, which breaks down a group into subgroups related to its prime factors. By analyzing these subgroups, we can assess the embeddability of the group into the wreath product. Notably, this approach yields a meaningful insight into the group structure, which can be utilized to identify group characteristics such as nilpotency, solvability, and finite order. Furthermore, this method enables us to derive explicit descriptions of group subgroups, including normal subgroups, Sylow subgroups, and the center of the group. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we provide a non-trivial example demonstrating how it can be applied to establish a group embedding into a wreath product. Additionally, we outline potential future directions for our research. By exploring various decomposition types, we can expand our approach to address more intricate group embedding issues. Moreover, this study paves the way for a broader examination of group properties utilizing the Cartesian decomposition framework. With this approach, we can tackle not just wreath products but also other complex group constructions, such as direct and semidirect products. Moreover, this study enables us to investigate group properties via the Cartesian decomposition framework, which can be applied to tackle complex group constructions, including direct and semidirect products, as well as vast families of group families, such as symmetric groups, alternating groups, and dihedral groups. Congenital heart defects pose a significant challenge in pediatric cardiac surgery, necessitating precise pre-surgical planning. However, medical experts often struggle to use standard imaging approaches for rare heart abnormalities. This study explores the potential of using a next-generation medical imaging technique called model-to-model transfer, which could make cardiac surgery more feasible and successful. By leveraging a type of artificial neural network called U-Net, researchers aim to enhance pre-surgical planning for complex heart surgeries involving rare congenital heart diseases. Our results show that using public datasets and a limited set of specialized training data, U-Net can effectively segment difficult-to-identify heart structures on patients with rare congenital heart diseases, even when those diseases are not represented in the training data. This research demonstrates the promise of medical experts collaborating with machine learning developers to create life-changing technologies for the medical community. Our approach also enables the development of a heart segmentation model that is adaptable, easy to update, and compatible with a wide range of computing systems. This innovation has the potential to create more efficient, low-cost cardiac surgery planning tools and could also pave the way for a community-driven development process across various fields. This study further highlights the potential of combining cutting-edge artificial intelligence techniques with self-supervised learning methods using public datasets, that can be leveraged to create life-changing technologies for the medical community. Our results, which show significant improvement over traditional heart segmentation methods, could also enable a new generation of low-cost, user-friendly, and high-performance cardiac surgery planning tools. This work has been recognized as one of the top submissions and has been selected as the best paper for the Medical and Health Science Applications session at the 2021 Conference. This paper has been selected for presentation at the Neural Information Processing Systems Conference 2021. For evaluation purposes, an independent group of experts in cardiac surgery reviewed and validated our results, which show a high level of accuracy when comparing predicted segmentations to actual heart structures, even in cases where the training data does not account for the specific congenital heart disease. This research has several key advancements, including the use of a relatively small number of specialized training data, a high level of accuracy when compared to other medical expert-validated segmentation methods, and significant breakthroughs in segmenting difficult-to-identify heart structures on patients with rare congenital heart diseases. Our proposed evaluation approach, comprehensive object evaluation (COE), 
encourages models to recognize a wide range of objects by incorporating 
additional object classes not used for classification. By exploring ways to 
include more diverse object classes in the evaluation, we investigate how COE 
can be tailored to better assess models' performance on specific recognition 
tasks. Our study reveals that a higher level of competition from unrelated 
objects does not necessarily translate to better performance, and that this 
effect varies depending on the dataset and the models being evaluated. 
Furthermore, we find that limiting COE to closely related object classes can 
be an effective way to improve models' performance on specific tasks, and 
frequently outperforms traditional evaluation methods in our experiments. 
Additionally, we observe that certain simple distortion techniques can be very 
effective at resisting sudden class discoveries, and we explore ways to 
incorporate more realistic testing conditions into the COE framework. By

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. We believe that leveraging both contextual and semantic information can greatly benefit our model in addressing this issue. In this research, we build upon the GlossBERT model by Huang et al., which combines contextual and semantic representations to improve the classification of word senses. We enhance their work by implementing multiple training methods, including parallel and systematic training of BERT and BERT-based structures, which results in a significant enhancement of their initial results. Our findings reveal that our approach yields state-of-the-art WSD performance, surpassing even the latest standards, which we make available on GitHub for reference. Moreover, our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of using both contextual and semantic information to address the WSD problem. We also explore various aspects of the Huang et al. model's vocabulary, including the relationship between the frequency of words and their corresponding sense inventories, as well as the distribution of primary and secondary senses across all word vocabularies. Our analysis uncovers striking patterns in the English language and provides valuable insights into the WordNet knowledge base. Our work paves the way for further advancements in the field of semantic representation through multi-task learning, while also highlighting the value of collaborative work between natural language processing and lexicography. Our research can serve as a reference for any future project dealing with the disambiguation of words. We utilize a publicly accessible dataset called SemCor, which is derived from the WordNet knowledge base, to evaluate our approach. This dataset is comprised of annotated texts containing a total of 33,885 word instances with different meanings. We employ a widely accepted evaluation metric called the accuracy score to assess the performance of our approach. Our results indicate a substantial improvement over the current state-of-the-art techniques, while also highlighting the beneficial effects of combining contextual and semantic information to achieve better word sense disambiguation. We successfully achieve an accuracy score of 57.14%, which represents a significant advancement of 6.14% over the standard baseline and 2.14% better than the latest competitor while using all available sense information. We also experiment with a more realistic scenario, where we only utilize a subset of the available sense information to demonstrate the robustness of our approach, while achieving a score of 56.25%. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a mix of written text and visual aids, which poses a significant challenge for the field of machine learning when attempting to train models that can learn about these procedures through guidebooks of any media type. Our key innovation in addressing this challenge is the concept of multimodal base cases (MBCs), which is a new representation that can learn about individual steps within a procedure by examining separate guidebook sections that are linked together. By developing a sequential model that combines MBCs and learns about step sequences, we were able to achieve impressive performance when tested against a range of procedural datasets compiled from online guidebooks, which show significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art models and confirms our proposed framework's effectiveness. Furthermore, our approach is robust when subjected to stress tests designed to evaluate its reliability in sequences that are more complex and varied. Our key approach, multimodal base cases, provides valuable insights into the underlying structural patterns that characterize procedural knowledge, which was previously unexplored. By applying structural pattern recognition and sequencing search, we were able to successfully use our model to gain a deeper understanding of real-world procedures, which was verified through a series of simple reasoning tests and more complex scenarios that involve reasoning about temporal common sense and multimodal information. Our model's ability to effectively learn about the Beatles' career by analyzing guidebooks of any media type is a notable example of its capabilities. One of the key advantages of our approach is its ability to handle a wide range of procedural knowledge expressions, which was demonstrated through a series of linguistic analyses and was found to consistently outperform the competition in every evaluated dataset. Our approach's robustness and ability to grasp the underlying structure of any procedure was confirmed when we successfully applied our model to a wide range of real-world procedures and communication methods, which was found to excel in every tested scenario. One of the key strengths of our approach is its simplicity, which was found to reduce the risk of model errors and enabled our model to successfully learn about the underlying structure of any procedure by utilizing a straightforward and easy-to-understand representation. One of the key areas where our approach could be improved is the development of a more sophisticated search algorithm that was found to impact search results in some tested scenarios. Our future research plans focus on addressing this limitation by exploring new search methods that will allow our model to efficiently learn about the underlying structure of any procedure.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this study delves into a more nuanced level by examining the distribution of removal impacts in network disruption. Specifically, we investigate this question using a binary opinion dynamics model on a randomly assembled Cayley tree network, and our findings reveal that the distribution of removal effects follows a power-law with an exponential cutoff, providing insights that can be utilized to refine immunization strategies. Additionally, our analysis identifies key factors that influence the distribution's parameters, such as the initial condition and the branching probability, offering directions for exploring other complex networks using similar statistical distribution methods. As a result, this study can help develop more targeted and effective network immunization methods. Furthermore, our approach is versatile, enabling us to analyze multiple metrics, such as influence assessment and spreading phenomena in various networks. Consequently, this study is valuable not only for resolving the specific issue of network vulnerability but also for solving other complex problems arising in social systems. In the context of the opinion dynamics model, our analysis unveils a clear relationship between the distribution of removal impacts and the model's basic components, such as the probability of false information dissemination and the reliability of message transmission. In addition, this study provides a quantitative basis for evaluating the efficacy of anti-spreading policies, in addition to revealing the intricate interplay between network architecture, dynamics, and the spectral radius. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the superiority of a nuanced, distribution-based approach to analyzing complex systems, producing results that, in some instances, contradict the predictions of established theoretical models. In the case of the opinion dynamics model, our analysis shows that the distribution of removal impacts always diverges from those predicted by the percolation theory, despite some overlap in magnitude. In conclusion, this study establishes a valuable paradigm for examining complex systems using a distribution-based analysis, a method that can be applied to other complex networks and may reveal similar breakthroughs. Furthermore, this study provides a clear framework for addressing one of the fundamental challenges associated with complex systems, namely the identification of a suitable time frame for evaluation. In the case of the opinion dynamics model, we determined that the most pertinent evaluation period is the one that corresponds to the longest surviving cascade. In addition, this study introduces a groundbreaking metric, known as the avalanche-magnitude distribution, that provides a clear and unbiased assessment of network vulnerability. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered by signal loss at high frequencies due to the slow decay of laser phase information. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the concept of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, which utilizes a heart-shaped test mass to split the laser phase into two segments. By significantly reducing the test mass's oscillation frequency, the interferometer achieves a ~100 times faster phase readout at high frequencies. Alternatively, a modified L-shaped test mass can achieve a ~10 times faster readout. Both designs can be implemented using advanced gravitational wave detector technology, offering the potential to recover signals at high frequencies. To evaluate this concept, we simulate signals from several astrophysical sources and find that the sloshing-Sagnac design can enhance the detection sensitivity of advanced gravitational wave detectors by a factor of ~10 at high frequencies. To incorporate this concept into future gravitational wave detectors, such as Einstein gravitational wave detector, we anticipate a ~10 times improvement in sensitivity at high frequencies, enabling the detection of more high-frequency signals. To realize this idea with current technology, however, would require a ~10 times larger mirror and a ~100 times larger power, respectively for the heart-shaped and L-shaped test masses. Nonetheless, this concept offers a viable path to enhancing the high frequency sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors. To further explore this idea, we propose the prototype demonstration of a heart-shaped Sagnac interferometer using a 30 cm diameter mirror, which we believe would provide a crucial proof of principle for the sloshing-Sagnac design. To that end, we outline a demonstration plan for the LIGO's Commissioning and Research Observatory, where we can conduct a thorough scientific test of this concept. By implementing this design, we can significantly enhance the detection capability of advanced gravitational wave detectors, especially for binary black hole and neutron star mergers involving objects with large mass ratios. Moreover, this technology can also be applied to optical interferometers used in searching for scalar gravitational waves and holographic measurements used in testing general relativity, thereby offering a wider range of scientific benefits. We discuss a new measure called'strength' or $\mathcal{S}$, which quantifies the normalization of a spectral distribution according to its overall magnitude. This analysis focuses on the 'Big Apple' – a special, unusually strong peak observed in the spectral distributions of finite nuclei, van der Waals molecules, and certain astrophysical objects. The available data indicate that $\mathcal{S}$ exceeds the expected maximum value for the Big Apple peak in momentum space, particularly in finite nuclei and van der Waals molecules. In the case of astrophysical objects, $\mathcal{S}$ falls within the predicted maximum value. A key aspect of this discussion is the relationship between the Big Apple peak and a quark-goldstone phenomenon. It is also shown that $\mathcal{S}$ directly correlates with the square of a spectral function's characteristic scale parameter $\xi$. A critical value of $\xi$ at approximately 1.1 governs the Big Apple's appearance, marking the boundary between a quark-goldstone regime and a collective regime. Furthermore, a universal $\xi$ value can serve as a critical parameter to understand the behavior of systems governed by the Big Apple dynamics. Ultimately, this analysis provides a universal framework for analyzing and comparing spectral distributions across finite and infinite systems. It also highlights the distinctive features of the Big Apple, underscoring its role as a hallmark of quark-goldstone physics. Consequently, systems that fail to exhibit the Big Apple peak, such as certain finite nuclei and astrophysical objects, are expected to possess alternative, collective dominant mechanisms governing their spectral distributions. A failure to recognize the Big Apple peak's significance might lead to incorrect interpretations of data, particularly in the study of finite nuclei and van der Waals molecules where the peak's strength exceeds expected maximum values. It is a critical aspect to differentiate between prolate and oblate configurations, as well as to account for any deviations from the predicted maximum value, by calculating the actual $\mathcal{S}$ value from the actual spectral distribution rather than relying on collective dominant assumptions. Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of choosing appropriate impurity models and pseudopotentials.  By resolving issues related to double counting of electron interactions, our study reveals the intricate relationship between band broadening, Mott-Hubbard splitting, and charge transfer energies.  According to our results, using a Kanamori-Linderstam model for all $d$ electrons overcorrects for band broadening, causing a shift in the phase diagram.  However, employing a two-band approach with distinct broadening and interaction parameters for $d$ and $p$ electrons provides a more comprehensive understanding, resulting in improved agreement with experimental data.  Furthermore, our analysis indicates that pseudopotential treatment can be seen as modeling $p$ electron inelastic scattering, demonstrating its impact on the phase diagram and the need to consider $p$-$d$ coupling in the interpretation of spectral functions. Our theoretical findings are complemented by numerical experiments, highlighting the advantages of linear models with few data points and small noise, as well as the challenges posed by larger noise levels. Our results demonstrate the superiority of linear models over neural networks in certain scenarios. Our analysis yields an interpretable feature selection, where the model is optimized using an extended gradient descent method. This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the context of network data. It outlines the challenges posed by publishing private graphs, the set of differential privacy mechanisms designed for graph data, including private subgraphs, and highlights the techniques for privately processing network data. Furthermore, it outlines potential research directions within this field. Initially, publishing private graphs presented considerable publication difficulties; however, the development of new tools to analyze graph algorithms privately has sparked renewed interest in this field. Private graphs can be categorized into non-publicized private graphs and published private graphs. The former encompasses private individuals whose connection history remains undisclosed, whereas the latter refers to individuals whose association with neighbors undergoes data transformation to ensure privacy. A further distinction is drawn within published private graphs, separating private edges whose connection strength is protected, and private node whose association history is protected. A significant body of work falls under private subgraphs, including private communities, where a user's connection to the entire graph is protected, and private cores, where a user's connection within a specific core is protected. Moreover, a substantial amount of work falls under graph data that is privately processed, encompassing private graph machine learning and private graph deep learning. This field is relatively underrepresented in literature when compared to other areas of research, and thus this paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of this field to inspire further exploration and contribution. Researchers have achieved a successful hydrodynamic description of quantum many-body systems by employing quantum hydrodynamics in combination with the Bogoliubov approximation. However, this approach falls short when studying out-of-equilibrium dynamics, particularly for systems where quantum fluctuations cannot be disregarded. To overcome these limitations, we present a novel application of phase-space Bogoliubov approximation quantum hydrodynamics. This method extends the applicability of this tool to any interacting Bose gas, enabling the representation of its dynamics through a set of closed quantum hydrodynamics equations that can be used to compute observables and nonequilibrium processes. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, we simulate the expansion of a one-dimensional Lieb-Liniger gas and compare our results to existing data, demonstrating a strong agreement. Furthermore, we investigate the nonequilibrium dynamics of a harmonic trap filled with MacNeil-like mixtures of $1$- and $3$-component Bose-Einstein condensates. Our approach also facilitates the investigation of quantum-fluctuation-dominated systems, such as thin atomic gases, enabling the prediction of Casimir forces and the formation of Bose-Einstein condensates in harmonic potentials. Additionally, we examine whether quantum-fluctuation effects can be incorporated into classical hydrodynamics, demonstrating that this is feasible in certain situations. Our findings provide a crucial framework for understanding the interplay between quantum fluctuations, interactions, and nonequilibrium dynamics in the behavior of interacting Bose gases. As such, this research is a significant step toward the development of a universal quantum-fluctuation-dominated hydrodynamic theory, which can be applied to any interacting Bose gas. Furthermore, this study offers a crucial basis for exploring the empirical application of this theory to real-world experiments with ultracold atomic gases, such that it can be put to use in accurately predicting the outcomes of out-of-equilibrium experiments. Our approach is a crucial contribution to the broader field of quantum hydrodynamics, enabling the representation of interacting Bose gases as equivalent systems that can be studied using either quantum hydrodynamics or Bogoliubov approximation, depending on the specific conditions of the given situation. As such, this research provides a model for uncovering the underlying principles that govern the behavior of more complex quantum many-body systems, such that it can be applied to any situation in which quantum fluctuations dominate the system's dynamics, whether in an equilibrium or nonequilibrium scenario. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of the PTM. However, the available data do not support this hypothesis, and the underlying mechanics of the PTM remain to be determined. A different viewpoint proposes that the PTM arise due to a specific configuration of the magnetic field coils used for ion cyclotron resonance frequency heating (ICRH). A numerical simulation demonstrated that the observed characteristics of the PLT could result from a field line caused by an ICRH coil, specifically one located near an edge localized mode's birthplace. A key aspect of this hypothesis is the fact that the starting point of the downflows associated with the PLT and ELMs shows a similar relationship to the major radius as that found for the PLT's magnetic footprint. A potential path forward for identifying the PTM in other tokamaks relies on a combined approach of observational data and numerical simulations. A previously overlooked link between the PLT and a specific magnetic field coil has significant implications for the interpretation of experimental data, underscoring the value of detailed, in-depth discussions between theorists and experimenters. A distinction must be drawn between causal relationships and those that appear correlated, a lesson that can be applied to a broader range of plasma problems. Their results demonstrated the existence of two-player Nash equilibria in their model, resulting in a focus on searching for a straightforward method to determine the approximate value of such equilibria. As part of their exploration, researchers developed a novel series of lower bounds related to model parameters, including the model's largest margin, defined as $\lambda_1$; the second-largest margin, defined as $\lambda_2$; and the shortest path distance between payoffs, defined as $\lambda_\infty$. Interestingly, the existing literature placed no upper bounds on the query complexity of finding a $\lambda_\infty$-equilibrium, despite it being a fundamental question in the field. In this work, the researchers establish a lower bound of $2^{2^{O(n)}}$ query complexity for finding a $\lambda_2$-equilibrium in Lipschitz games for any $\lambda_2\geq 2$, based on a series of lower bounds derived from reducing the problem of finding a $\lambda_2$-equilibrium to that of finding a $\lambda_\infty$-equilibrium. Furthermore, further investigation is needed to determine the feasibility of obtaining more manageable upper bounds or specific cases with lower bounds. Additionally, this work introduces a novel concept of $\lambda$-monotonic payoffs, resulting in a $O(\lambda n)$-equivalent transformation, along with a $\lambda$-generalization of coarsening networks, resulting in $\lambda$-Lipschitz Boolean matrices. To examine the impact of Google's web search personalisation on users' ability to discover relevant information, we conducted six scenarios in which 5,000 search queries were artificially generated and sent to Google's web search with the display of up to ten results per page. The investigation showed that when search engines display more results and Google's web search personalisation is disabled, users can discover 21% more relevant information, reducing the gap by half when the display of results is increased to ten pages. Moreover, if users are given access to all relevant information, the difference decreases to 12%. Notably, the disparity persists even if users are given access to all relevant information, indicating that considerable amounts of relevant information may be concealed due to Google's web search personalisation. To put this into perspective, for a typical web search with five displayed results and no access to hidden information, only 58% of all relevant information can be discovered. The study's findings have implications for web search companies, non-profit organisations, and government agencies that rely on web search as a means of disseminating information to the public. To improve the discovery of relevant information, we propose several guidelines, including providing users with the option to disable web search personalisation, displaying more search results, and clearing web search cookies before critical interactions. The study's findings are significant, with potential applications beyond web search, as they offer insight into the phenomenon of suppressed visibility, where the concealment of information from users with privileged access can result in the hidden, cumulative effects of numerous individual instances. The empirical evidence provided can facilitate the development of more effective strategies for enhancing the discovery of relevant information, as well as informing policy decisions in areas where web search personalisation has implications for web search companies' business models, internet freedom, civic engagement, and the distribution of online resources. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging graph structures and node features to make informed decisions. However, GNNs often comprise numerous parameters, complicating their understanding and making them prone to manipulation. To address these challenges, we propose a novel technique called Learned Sparsification, which reduces unnecessary GNN connections while maintaining network performance. By incorporating a $p$-sparsity constraint into the optimization process, Learned Sparsification identifies the most crucial edges in the graph that contribute significantly to the network's parameters. We demonstrate Learned Sparsification's effectiveness by integrating it into popular GNN architectures, resulting in a notable decrease in parameters and improved accuracy on various datasets, including Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed. Notably, our method surpasses existing sparsification techniques and even achieves state-of-the-art performance in certain cases. Through extensive experiments, we show Learned Sparsification's ability to identify interpretable subgraphs that underlie the model's predictions, highlighting the potential for this method to facilitate human understanding of GNNs. We also explore the integration of Learned Sparsification into classification networks and find it can be a powerful tool for uncovering crucial graph elements that inform the model's decisions. By examining Learned Sparsification through both a theoretical and a practical lens, we contribute a novel approach that efficiently reduces unnecessary GNN connections while ensuring the network's interpretability. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories, with a focus on the collider's sensitivity to beyond-Standard Model Higgs interactions. Our analysis considers the most relevant operators affecting Higgs boson interactions and compares Higgs pair production channels, weighing their discovery potential and mass determination accuracy. To illustrate the influence of BSM interactions, we choose a set of BSM parameters that serve as a reference point, then examine how our findings change under different BSM parameter variations. Our study shows that the most sensitive production process is double Higgs production via a $WW$ contact, followed by final state decay into bottom quarks. For the CLIC collider, this process allows for the detection of double Higgs production with a 0.17 TeV sensitivity, while mass sensitivity for this process reaches 0.25 TeV. In the ILC case, we find a 0.29 Te V sensitivity for this process, and study the optimal beam energies to achieve this performance. Furthermore, we investigate the combined effect of BSM interactions on Higgs pair production processes, as well as Higgs-strahlung processes, demonstrating that in the ILC case, a 0.30 TeV sensitivity for double Higgs production holds when considering BSM-induced shifts in the Higgs peak position. Our study highlights the significance of precise Higgs peak profile measurements at these colliders, along with potential improvements in sensitivity that could result from combining Higgs pair production and Higgs-strahlung processes. Our analysis provides key input for the development of optimal experimental strategies for detecting double Higgs production, as well as BSM interactions, at these electron-positron colliders. This study has been carried out within the framework of the ILC/CLIC Detector Concept Study, led by the CLIC Detector Concept Study Group, and we anticipate our findings to contribute to the ongoing development of the ILC Research Direction and the CLIC CDR. Additionally, this analysis has been submitted to be presented at the 2022 Lepton Photon Conference. 

This work has been done in collaboration with the CLIC Detector Concept Study Group, and the ILC/CLIC Detector Concept Study Group.

The development of highly advanced driving robots depends on the creation of realistic traffic scenarios through generation methods. Current approaches using neural networks to produce traffic scenes suffer from limitations such as rigid layout formation, the absence of dynamic elements like traffic participators, and an unrealistic distribution of road types. Furthermore, traditionally-trained models struggle to generalize beyond the datasets used for training, resulting in models that, while capable of processing images, cannot utilize this ability to inform the generation of traffic scenes. We introduce SceneGen, a traffic scene model based on conditionally sequence generators that is capable of creating a wide variety of realistic traffic scenes through the integration of learned distributions of all scene components, including dynamic participants and types of road. SceneGen is trained using a dataset composed of collected real-world traffic scenes and becomes expertly skilled at reproducing these scenes through the use of only scene labels. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We demonstrate the capability of this model to achieve precise classification results on the MNIST dataset, achieving an accuracy of 98.12%. Furthermore, we showcase the significant reduction in energy consumption, amounting to a 10,000 times decrease, when comparing our proposed model to a traditional neural network implementation. We also explore the relationship between energy expenditure and classification performance, revealing that there is an optimal balance between spikes per neuron and accuracy. To facilitate replication and further research, an open-source implementation of this model is available for download. We anticipate that this variant of the Random Neural Network, incorporating spike-based computation, will serve as a role model for the development of next-generation multiclass classifiers. We have made adjustments to address reviewer feedback, including modification of the energy efficiency measurement method, addition of a new training protocol, and inclusion of comparative results with other neuromorphic classifiers. These changes demonstrate the ability of this classifier to achieve similar accuracy with significantly reduced spikes. Additionally, we have expanded the dataset to include real-world image data, proving that this model can successfully classify elements from various datasets. Lastly, we have addressed concerns regarding the limited number of training episodes by showcasing the model's performance with an increased number of training episodes, revealing that it is capable of achieving 99.52% accuracy. We have also clarified the model's energy efficiency metrics, modified the classification protocol, and included further examples of the model's applicability. We have made the open-source code more versatile, enabling it to handle multiple datasets with a single training session. We have also included a new section discussing the model's potential applications and future areas for research. We have modified the classification protocol to utilize a more standardized approach, adapted the model to utilize a spiking linear layer, and included results demonstrating the model's ability to achieve 99.52% accuracy with real-world image data. Within an augmented Standard Model, we introduce a $B-L$ gauge boson, $Z_{\text{B-L}}$, and six scalar boson components from one complex $SU(2)_L$ scalar doublet. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by gradually accelerating their rotation. This acceleration, caused by solar radiation pressure, results in a speed increase that can be measured to estimate the asteroids' physical characteristics. By analyzing three asteroids - (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos - the researchers have provided the first data to demonstrate the YORP effect's influence on their rotational velocities. These findings suggest that (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro are experiencing a speed increase due to the YORP effect, while (1620) Geographos, despite initially being a non-principal axis rotator, is likely to convert to a such state as a result of this effect over a time period of approximately one century. The data also reveal that (10115) 1992 SK, with a low equatorial mass anomaly and a long axis that is not clearly defined as an extreme prolateness, may be an irregularly shaped asteroid. These discoveries are significant in understanding how the YORP effect influences asteroids' rotational velocities and could provide valuable insights for future observational campaigns. Furthermore, the analysis highlights the importance of precisely tracking asteroids' rotational velocities over time. The YORP effect's impact can be measured by analyzing the asteroids' light curves, a technique that can be enhanced by a combination of ground-based observations and data from the Lucas telescope, which is equipped with a high-speed photometer capable of monitoring large near-Earth asteroids' light curves. The Lucas telescope is set to provide continuous coverage of these asteroids, as well as others of this kind, and is expected to significantly contribute to the field of small body research. The data analyzed in this study were obtained from the IA2 system, which allows for real-time analysis and the rapid publication of results, a capability that the team believes will be crucial for identifying transient phenomena such as the YORP effect-induced rotational state changes in asteroids. The IA2 system is based on the previous version known as the IA system, which provided the basis for the results presented in this study. We investigate line ripple formations at normal incidence on two-dimensional gold patches of varying sizes, studying their resonance characteristics.  Both numerical simulations and theoretical calculations confirm the results.  The findings indicate that line ripples only occur when there are two distinct resonances with a significant difference in their strengths, a phenomenon that may be engineered through the design of these gold patches.  By modifying the size of these patches, we can adjust the wavelengths at which the line ripples form, as well as the orientations of the ripples.  Our research presents several potential applications for line ripples in both negative refractive index materials and Babinet's equivalent systems, particularly in the visible range.  To support line ripples with THz waves, we propose a design involving a dual metasurface, consisting of small patches on one side and large patches on the other.  Both numerical simulations and experimental measurements verify that this design can indeed support line ripples in the THz frequency range.  We also explore the possibility of controlling line ripples through slight misalignments between the two halves of the dual metasurface, confirming that even minute changes can significantly affect the ripples.  Our research indicates that line ripples can arise in deep sub-wavelength systems, presenting an intriguing contrast to the conventional view that such systems are incapable of supporting line ripples.  By applying a transfer matrix approach to our design, we derive a condition known as the '2T-2L criterion,' which specifies that a 2-dimensional system must possess two types of resonances with distinct characteristics in order to support line ripples.  Our study provides a clear path for the design of line ripples in optical frequencies, enabling the creation of line ripples in deep sub-wavelength systems through suitable choice of the dimensions of small and large patches.  Finally, we investigate how line ripples interconnect with another phenomenon, Coherent Phase Change (CPC), confirming that they share a common origin and presenting the '2T-2L 4-block matrix criterion' that must be met for a system to exhibit either CPC or line ripples.  Our research paves the way for the design of line ripples in optical frequencies, while also establishing a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms that give rise to this phenomenon.  By recognizing that line ripples result from the interplay between two contrasting resonances, we can now harness this understanding to control line ripples in a deliberate manner, thereby enabling the intentional creation of line ripples in deep sub-wavelength systems.

This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame from a specified set, subject to state and control constraints. We've also derived a new way to solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation by approximating the Hamiltonian's next-state function using Cauchy-type integrals, which can be used to calculate reachability levels on a grid. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of our method by finding the states that can be reached within two seconds from the origin for a simple example, and the results improve as the sampling rate increases. Notably, our approach determines the optimal policy required to reach the calculated states, and we've observed that these policy values align with those obtained from an off-the-shelf tool applied to the same problem. However, our new method allows us to explicitly remove this issue, thereby

efficient, capable of handling large data sets with an notable level of precision.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like Long Tuned and ALBERT.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based enhancement framework known as CTG@RT, which employs related tasks and instances to refine models.
The framework goes through multiple iterations, using a set of fixed retrieval methods to gradually update models in accordance with their performance.
The results of our experiments indicate that the proposed framework yields significant improvements in cross-task generalization, and its source code is now available for public access. Moreover, the investigation of its components reveals that the selection of models to be transferred has a substantial impact on performance. The updated code can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/CTG-RT, and the models obtained through CTG@RT can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/CTG-RT-models. When creating private machine learning models, a balance must be struck between minimizing the leakage of sensitive information and achieving satisfactory model performance. However, the process of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) for private machine learning models is complicated by the noise added to training data, which obscures the usual performance indicators used for HPO. As a result, existing HPO methods may no longer be effective in the private setting. To address this challenge, a new hyperparameter optimization framework called Private Hyperparameter Optimization (PHO) is proposed, combining elements of efficient HPO techniques with privacy-preserving methods. Specifically, PHO utilizes a reduced model to facilitate swift hyperparameter evaluations, while leveraging a differentially private neighbor discovery mechanism to enhance the efficiency of hyperparameter searches. Through experiments on multiple private deep learning scenarios, PHO demonstrates significant improvements over current HPO methods, highlighting the potential of PHO to optimize private model performance accurately. The proposed framework is now open-sourced for the community to utilize, with potential applications extending beyond deep learning and embracing a broader spectrum of machine learning models. The code is available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-NeuSoft/private-hpo, where further information on PHO can be found. As the field of private machine learning continues to evolve, the future of PHO is bright, with numerous research avenues awaiting exploration and contribution from both the hyperparameter optimization and private machine learning communities. As a landmark work, this paper is expected to pave the way for the development of more sophisticated hyperparameter optimization methods that can tackle various challenges in private machine learning settings. The problem of finding a linear differential equation whose solutions share specific mean value properties, particularly one related to Q-curvature, is a key area of inquiry in the field of partial differential equations. This note presents an investigation into whether such differential equations can be established for linear operators when the domain under consideration is a domain within R^n with smooth boundaries. The focus is on determining whether the given equation can be formulated when the mean value property is defined by means of the Gauss map and geodesic rays. The results obtained in this investigation are presented in the form of theorems. The techniques employed in the proof of these theorems involve exploiting the properties of the Gauss map, set differentiation, and the use of Minkowski geometric measure to characterize sets with a smooth boundary. The results provided in this note address questions recently posed by T. Hagstrom and T. Weaver. Epidemics like the current opioid epidemic in the US necessitate a thorough understanding of factors contributing to drug consumption risk. While research into the topic has yielded various predictors, there is still a need to identify robust, evidence-based indicators to enhance prediction accuracy. Interestingly, recent studies have demonstrated that the Five Factor Model (FFM) of personality can serve as a useful framework for predicting individuals susceptible to illicit drug consumption. However, the results of previous research have varied depending on factors such as population sampled, specific drug examined, and assessment tools used. To address this issue, the current study employed a combined approach, utilizing both exploratory and confirmatory research methods to examine the relationship between the FFM and consumption risk, while also considering potential moderating effects based on gender. The study's participants consisted of 498 college students, who completed a range of assessments including the NEO-PI-3, Drug Abuse Screening Test, and Impulsivity Inventory. The results revealed significant associations between certain personality traits and consumption risk, with the effects varying depending on the specific drug assessed and gender of the participant. Notably, neuroticism emerged as a primary predictor of increased consumption risk across all drugs, while extraversion exhibited a positive relationship with alcohol and cannabis consumption risk and a negative one with prescription drug misuse. In contrast, conscientiousness minimized consumption risk only for prescription drugs, whereas open-minded individuals displayed elevated risk for marijuana consumption and those with high agreeableness scores had a heightened risk for cannabis and opioid consumption. The study's findings highlight the value of considering personality traits within the context of the FFM to better understand the complex factors contributing to consumption risk. Furthermore, the results suggest that targeting specific personality traits through tailored interventions can potentially reduce consumption risk. In addition, the study reveals the limitations of prior research characterized by a focus on exploratory analyses, and emphasizes the importance of employing confirmatory research to validate findings, especially in the complex field of psychology. Finally, the study indicates that in order to move the field forward, researchers should adopt a theory-driven approach to the design of future studies.

We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. Our work builds upon prior research and offers improved solutions for achieving uncloneable encryption. Prior research employed a unique approach involving an uncloneable function as a fundamental component, with which they demonstrated uncloneable encryption was feasible. In contrast, our work demonstrates that uncloneable encryption can be achieved even in the absence of such a component, using either a weak uncloneable function or a non-interactive public key system. Furthermore, we identify the minimal requirements for a component that can enable uncloneable encryption, specifically, it must possess both the property of a weak uncloneable function and that of a non-interactive public key system. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative regularization methods. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward, and the approach demonstrates robust performance across multiple datasets and model configurations. The code for our experiments is openly accessible. Through our analysis of the effects of the model's Lipschitz constant on its performance, we discovered that smaller constants result in better performance, although below a certain threshold this improvement is nullified due to increased bias. The findings of this study can be applied across a wide range of machine learning models, as we demonstrate through a simple example. We found that enforcing a model's Lipschitz continuity can be a viable strategy for model regularization, capable of outperforming established methods like dropout and weight decay. The advantages of this approach, in terms of hyperparameter selection, lack of additional parameters and simplicity in implementation, make it a compelling model regularization technique. The results of this study can be applied across a wide range of machine learning models, as we demonstrate through a simple example. Their sequential design leads to fundamental challenges when working with
inflected languages that employ agglutinative morphological structures.
Our analysis indicates that current state-of-the-art models, including an
LSTM-based model, struggle to effectively process morphological features
due to their limited ability to maintain context over a series of suffixes.
To illustrate this issue, we use Basque as an example, presenting a
systematic analysis of its complex inflection system and providing evidence
from both syntactic and lexical perspectives to support our findings.
Our research suggests that developing new network architectures capable
of managing context across a range of suffixes will be crucial for
effectively processing agglutinative languages that employ a similar
concordance system found in Basque. Furthermore, we believe that such
innovations in network architecture will also have a positive impact on the
performance of models in tasks that rely on the interpretation of context,
both within Basque and across other agglutinative languages. To facilitate

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, offers scientists a valuable opportunity to study its substantial effects on the planet's atmosphere during its close approach. With the upcoming launch of the James Webb Telescope, researchers will be able to analyze the planet's behavior as it closely approaches its star. However, to make the most out of this observational data, it is crucial to update the planet's orbital schedule with the highest level of accuracy possible. By gathering new data from a global network of telescopes, we were able to refine the planet's orbital calendar and ensure that the James Webb Telescope is scheduled to observe it during its closest approach.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches has primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside the original distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thereby enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. This research lays the groundwork for the development of deep learning models capable of enhancing PET images using lower doses without relying on specific training datasets, which can be a crucial breakthrough in making PET scans more accessible to a broader population. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) examines how parts of a conversation are organized, with implications for both the structure of human language and how people comprehend language. This paper delves into the connection between CT and the technology used to solve coreference problems, such as identifying the noun "she" refers to in the sentence "she is going to the store." As coreference resolution systems based on neural networks consistently perform well, the relationship between CT and these systems warrants investigation. By analyzing various coreference resolution systems, including ones that use pre-trained neural networks, we found that they can accurately identify the focus of a sentence. However, their ability to determine the connections between sentences is more variable and often fails to replicate the relationships identified by CT. In extension to this, we developed a new evaluation metric centered on the principles of CT, which further highlighted the discrepancies between these systems and human judgment. The full dataset and all models examined in this study have been made publicly available. Investigating the impact of modifying a coreference resolution system to align with CT-driven priorities showed that such changes results in only a minor decline in overall performance, indicating that simple adjustments can lead to systems better reflecting the aspects of human language captured by CT. As a result, this work contributes to the exploration of the relationship between human language and the technology used to solve coreference problems, along with the development of a more nuanced evaluation metric for coreference resolution systems. Furthermore, it highlights potential directions for further research in both the fields of natural language processing and human language. In the context of NLP, it raises questions about the reliance on systems that, despite performing well, differ from human language, as well as potential paths to creating more human-like language based on combining various linguistic theories. In the field of human language, it suggests investigating how people comprehend language with a focus on coreference, along with the design of more effective teaching methods using coreference-related aspects of human language, as well as how to express these aspects in a more accessible way. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling design choices on the instability in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This work builds upon existing research by examining the factors influencing regenerative beam breakup instability, specifically when the beam and the electromagnetic field in the RF cavity are both synchronized with the RF frequency, taking into consideration the effects of detector locations, cavity voltage, and emittance. Numerical simulations were conducted for a 3 GeV energy recovery linac using a multi-particle beam model, and the results showed that the instability can be mitigated by increasing the detector location from 70 meters to 140 meters, reducing the required emittance by three to four times. However, this comes at the cost of increased power losses in the cavity. Additionally, the research demonstrated that a larger detector placement can compensate for an increase in cavity voltage, eliminating the constraint it imposes on the filling design. Furthermore, it was observed that a 1:7 ratio between the beam and RF periods can reduce the power loss by half, compared to the 1:4 ratio commonly adopted in proton accelerators. The study provides a detailed analysis of power loss components, breaking them down into fundamental sources. It also introduces a new figure of merit for filling design, the effective particle charge, that takes account of both single-pass and multi-pass beam breakup instability, as well as power loss, to offer a comprehensive evaluation of filling design choices. Ultimately, the research lays the groundwork for the exploration of larger beam currents in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. The study's findings may also be applicable to future light source Stewart platforms, which require large emittances to achieve the necessary low-loss thresholds. Imitation learning has become a influential approach in robotics for its simplicity in training policies without the need for explicit reward functions. However, imposing complex task dependencies and avoiding obstacles in a robot's movement adds significant difficulty to the imitation learning process. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a novel imitation learning framework called EKMP, which extends beyond basic imitation learning capabilities. EKMP utilizes multiple types of expert demonstrations, including those with linear and nonlinear constraints, as well as demonstrations that avoid specific areas, to guide a robot's movement to achieve complex task objectives. By formulating a series of reformulated constraints based on expert feedback, EKMP runs efficient optimization processes to find a solution that meets all demonstration specifications. Our research has resulted in three main variations of the EKMP framework: a version for linear constraints, a version for nonlinear constraints and a version for avoiding specific areas. Through thorough experimentation, we have demonstrated EKMP's effectiveness in training a robot arm to perform a series of complex tasks using only visual observations. Our work represents a significant contribution to the development of more sophisticated imitation learning algorithms capable of handling complex nonlinear constraints and learning from expert demonstrations that avoid specific areas, which has important implications for its application in real-world robotics applications. By utilizing sensitive resistivity measurements, we have found a previously unreported phenomenon in the vortex state of the doped manganite Pr$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. Here, upon doping, the vortex lattice transition from a square arrangement to a grid-like pattern can be observed. This discovery offers a new means by which to study the interplay between two kinds of charge order present in these materials and provides a method for adjusting the stability of the grid-like vortex state. Here, we also provide an explanation for this transition based on the interaction between superconducting currents and antiphase N\'{e}el order, suggesting that this transition could serve as a phase diagram reference point for studying competing orders in other superconducting materials. Notably, this study reveals that the grid-like vortex state can be stabilized through magnetic field alignment, achieving this transition at higher temperatures than previously reported. Finally, we propose that the grid-like vortex state could end in one of two possible transitions, either to a triangular lattice or a small-angle spiral, either of which could be realized through appropriate adjustment of doping level or material composition.

We introduce a new dimension concept called the trimmed metric dimension for undirected graphs, where the dimension is calculated using a subset of the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices. Specifically, we identify the smallest number $k$ such that there exist $k$ vertices $S$ in the graph $G$ for which the distance between any two vertices in $G$ can be determined using only the shortest paths to the vertices in $S$, excluding the paths with length more than half of the maximum shortest path length in $G$. We also provide a method to determine the trimmed metric dimension of a graph by removing unnecessary vertices from the set $S$. Moreover, some lower and upper bounds for the trimmed metric dimension of graphs are established. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the trimmed metric dimension and other graph parameters, including the graph's minimum dominating set, vertex cover, and the smallest set of vertices whose all other vertices have a neighbor in this set. Finally, we calculate or estimate the trimmed metric dimension of several graph classes, including cycles, trees, series-parallel graphs, and Cartesian products of graphs. The notion of trimmed metric dimension can be applied to dynamic and temporal graphs as well. It exhibits a unique Y-shaped geometry with varied interior basin dimensions.  Pre-rift crust in this region is estimated to be around 2-3 km in thickness.  Based on data from the Deep Sea Drill Project Site 351A located in the Walvis Ridge and obtained magnetic anomaly dates, the Southern Atlantic rifting phase occurred between 132 and 126 million years ago.  This was followed by passive margin breakup in the E-W to NE-SW trending South Atlantic segment between 126 and 126 Ma, with the alpha, beta, and gamma chron units corresponding to 124.51, 124.02, and 123.19 Ma respectively.  Initial rifting in this region is dated at around 132 Ma, with subsequent break-up and continental drift occurring between 126 and 123 Ma.  The time elapsed for this process varied from 6 million years in the western segment to 8 million years in the eastern segment. The success of models like Multi-Label Network (MLN) and Multi-Label Graph Convolutional Network (MLGCN) relies heavily on their ability to process a large number of labeled samples. However, working with a vast number of labeled samples can be challenging, if not impossible, for many real-world applications. In contrast, they often have access to extensive datasets with single-label annotations. This paper investigates whether it's possible to create a multi-label dataset from these single-label annotations, assuming the model has no access to additional labeled data. Our proposed approach, Resampling Based on Single Positive Labels (RBSPL), involves reassigning existing single-positive labels to multiple labels, based on the model's prediction. We validate RBSPL through a series of experiments on publicly available multi-label classification datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing high-quality multi-label datasets. The code for our method is publicly available on GitHub. Our findings indicate that models trained on datasets created using RBSPL outperform those trained on the original single-label datasets. This is consistent with our initial hypothesis that RBSPL can create efficient multi-label learning pathways for models like MLN and MLGCN, even in the absence of additional labeled data. This could result in significant reductions in the cost associated with annotating datasets, making RBSPL a valuable tool for multi-label research. In addition to verifying the effectiveness of RBSPL, we also conducted a comparative analysis of different techniques that utilize single-positive labels to create multi-label datasets. Academic researchers who read research papers usually do so to stay informed, but they often spend precious time browsing through papers solely to remember key facts they have previously learned. Rather than re-discovering well-established information, these readers could be learning new concepts from the latest developments. Unfortunately, discovering what they already know requires significant time, hindering the efficiency of their knowledge updates. To address this problem, a new search function has been developed that allows users to specify whether a particular fact should be confirmed as true or false. To evaluate the performance of this new search function, a diverse group of advanced graduate students was asked to search for particular facts related to twenty research papers in the field of Computer Science, with twenty additional students verifying the results they obtained. To assess the precision of the new search function, these students were also asked to identify whether the fact they found was indeed present in the corresponding section of the paper, with nearly all of the students (98%) confirming that the fact they found was indeed mentioned in the paper. Furthermore, the results showed that the new search function was able to find the desired fact in nearly half of the cases (44%), with the remaining cases being those where the fact could be deduced by combining the information presented in the paper, with the exception of two instances where the paper contained opposing views on the fact in question. To make the results of this evaluation reproducible, the data used in the evaluation has been made available in the form of a diverse group of query-answer pairs related to research papers, with each query representing a specific fact that was searched for, along with the corresponding answer provided by the new search function, as well as the decision made by the corresponding student regarding the validity of the fact, with the exception of two instances where the paper contained opposing views on the fact question. Unfortunately, the issue of having to re-read the same words over and over again cannot be resolved by the new search function, but it can still provide a solution to the problem of discovering what one already knows about a particular concept. To take full advantage of the benefits it offers, it is essential to compare the results it provides with those obtained from re-reading the same words over and over again. To achieve this, a new metric has been proposed that assesses the performance of the new search function in finding facts that can be deduced by combining the information presented in the paper, with the aim of establishing a new standard for evaluating the effectiveness of this type of technology in the future. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. Our analysis reveals that in the presence of the linear potential, the Majorana fermion exhibits the behavior of a charge that is directly proportional to the difference between the fermion's position and its maximum or minimum possible location. This relationship allows the particle's entropy to be interpreted as a function of the square of its momentum. As a result, the thermodynamic behavior of the Majorana fermion can be seen as equivalent to that of a free particle with a linear potential influencing its momentum. This analysis establishes that the linear relationship between the Majorana fermion's entropy and the square of its momentum holds not just statistically but universally. Consequently, we can confidently leverage this linear correlation to accurately predict the Majorana fermion's thermodynamic behavior. This understanding may be applied to the thermodynamics of zero-dimensional systems, where entropy can be used to determine the linear relationship between the Majorana fermion's momentum and its potential, thereby allowing us to regulate its behavior. This finding can further be utilized to validate the proposed method for controlling the critical temperature of systems mediated by Majorana fermions by adjusting their entropy. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This platform can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the project's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. This system, though initially conceived to accommodate acronyms in the biomedical field, has demonstrated potential in handling acronyms in the scientific domain as well. To evaluate MadDog's performance, a set of comprehensive tests has been conducted, with the added feature of user feedback integration to further improve its overall effectiveness. With the constantly evolving nature of language dictionaries, acronyms, and the ongoing generation of new texts, it is essential to recognize that this system is not devoid of flaws and there is a clear need for continuous refinement to ensure its optimal functioning. As such, we welcome any suggestions or contributions from the academic community to enhance MadDog's capabilities. This system has the potential to contribute positively to various text-based applications, such as text summarization, information extraction, and discovery of hidden concepts within texts. By providing this kind of functionality within a comprehensive system, encompassing both identification and disambiguation capabilities, we believe we have created a ground-breaking approach that can be incorporated into various text preprocessing methods. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that separate the momentum space into distinct regions with differential spin transport. Notably, topological insulators that lack a bulk gap can display nodal lines - one-dimensional trajectories where energy remains constant across interconnecting points in momentum space. This line's existence relies on a key concept: the Wannier-Zak map, which derives an integral quantity (a topological invariant) from a discrete integral of a system's Hamiltonian using a specific basis set. While this approach is generally effective, it faces challenges when applied to high-dimensional momentum spaces. A topological invariant, known as the Wilson-Plochinger (WP) dual, has been developed to overcome these difficulties, specifically for 2D and 3D Dirac fermion systems. A negative WP dual value indicates the presence of a nodal line, providing a universal framework for identifying these topological states. Notably, nodal lines can also emerge in photonic and phononic systems, where a negative WP dual value serves as a robust indicator of their realization. A key aspect of these systems is the utility of electronic/photonic/phononic Hamiltonians that exhibit symmetry-protected nodal lines, providing a framework for the design of topological systems across different wave types. Recent examples of nodal lines are presented, drawn from both theoretical models and real-world systems, including a 3D Dirac fermion system based on van der Waals bonding, a 2D graphene system, a 1D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, and a topological phononic system. These examples demonstrate the practical application of the WP dual concept in identifying nodal lines, paving the way for their realization in photonic and other systems. A negative WP dual value serves as a universal indicator of nodal lines, unaffected by the type of wave being studied. This breakthrough in the detection of nodal lines is a significant step towards their deliberate creation in designed systems, enabling unprecedented control over topological phenomena. Developing short-term weather forecasts remains a key challenge, and a common approach is using numerical weather prediction models such as the Global Forecast System (GFS) model. A key factor in these models' performance is the resolution of the forecast, which affects the prediction of storms and other weather phenomena. Despite the high computational powers available today, solving these models explicitly within the forecast period is still not feasible due to the limitations imposed by the stability of the method. A key restriction is the CFL condition, which dictates that the grid size must be significantly smaller than the forecast period, further limiting the achievable resolution. This project proposes an innovative method for rapid water surface height and velocity solutions using deep learning, where data is fed into the model at a higher temporal frequency than the forecast period. Another key aspect of this project is the development of a new shallow water equations solver known as the Deep Rapid Shallow Water (DRSW) method, which utilizes a novel transformation of the conservative form of the equations to provide an alternative formulation suitable for deep learning optimization. Furthermore, the project includes the creation of a novel training tool, where the DRSW method is reformulated as a transformation of the conserved variables, which enables the use of the original conservative form of the equations.
