This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive study is being conducted to examine how different variables such as muscle fiber orientation, boundary constraints, and material properties affect the performance of the BDDC/AMG solver. Specifically, the investigation assesses how these variables influence key BDDC/AMG metrics including convergence rate, degree of freedom, and communication volume. Furthermore, the project is conducting a comparative analysis of the scalability of the BDDC/AMG method on Infiniband and GPU clusters. The research utilizes the Cray XE6 and Xeon E5-2690 architectures for its computations. By examining how different degrees of parallelization influence performance, the project aims to provide recommendations for optimizing the configuration of heart simulation simulations. The study is also exploring potential improvements to the BDDC solver for further enhancing the efficiency of the heart simulation model. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent drawback of traditional softmax formulation when modeling uncertainty. The problem with the softmax function is that it consistently outputs probabilities that, when summed, equal 1, yet this does not account for instances where the classification is uncertain and a new category exists. To address this shortcoming, a novel quantitative uncertainty measure is proposed, derived from the energy-based network's pairwise similarity computation. This new uncertainty measure serves as a complement to the classification output and is designed using a separate energy-based detector. To account for the open-world scenario, where the assessment of uncertainty is not limited to the existing categories, a new type of outlier sample is proposed. A new loss function is also introduced to the energy-driven uncertainty model, allowing it to learn in an open-world setting. One of the key limitations in applying spatial mode demultiplexing for optical quantum communications is the difficulty in overcoming the entanglement breaking effect caused by beam splitter coupling. This challenge becomes particularly pronounced when attempting to separate spatially entangled photons through a beam splitter without reducing the signal-to-noise ratio. While conventional methods rely on a large number of samples or angular resolution greater than one FSR to achieve this goal, our research demonstrates a significant breakthrough. By employing a data-driven approach utilizing machine learning and a specific training process, we are able to efficiently demultiplex spatial modes even under the most challenging conditions, where the angular separation between modes is an extremely fine fraction of one FSR. This remarkable achievement was showcased through the execution of a complex quantum channel coding task using a beam splitter with a high ratio of channel width to FSR. Our findings may also pave the way for the development of efficient and accurate spatial mode demultiplexing techniques in accounts where a large number of samples may not be obtainable, thereby expanding the potential applications of spatial mode demultiplexing in optical quantum communications. Our work is a preliminary outcome of the South Korea-Chinese Quantum Science and Technology Meeting 2021. While our initial results demonstrated improvement, further optimization is required to fully utilize the presented protocol's capabilities. Additionally, our research indicates that machine learning can enhance classical applications involving beam splitters, resulting in the suggestion of a potential collaboration with the Korean Advanced Research Laboratory (KARL). Our team is already exploring the integration of machine learning with quantum communications, inspired by the words of I.I. Rabi, "The only way to do great work is to love what you do." Leveraging machine learning to optimize quantum communications tasks aligns with the advice given to one of us by Professor Rabi. Our work on this project was performed under the supervision of Prof. S. Lanfredi from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro and supported by the following funding sources: the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development (CNPQ), the Rio de Janeiro State Research Council (FAPERJ), and the University of Sydney. Our team expresses gratitude to Prof. R. Hanson from the University of Sydney and Prof. R. R. King from the National Science Foundation for providing access to essential equipment and invaluable guidance. We would also like to extend our appreciation to the anonymous reviewers whose constructive feedback contributed to the improvement of this manuscript. Our research on this project is ongoing, with the goal of achieving optimal performance using reduced-scale versions of complex quantum communications

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is crucial. This work focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode pattern, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals that the model's mixed-mode oscillations, preceding a large amplitude oscillation, can switch between two different, concatenated patterns of oscillations. Furthermore, the model's detection mechanism for large amplitude oscillations, based on the normal form, can also identify the switching behavior mentioned above. This mechanism, however, loses its ability to detect the oscillations' underlying cause, i.e., the model's specific parameter values. In contrast, the model's operator theorem-based detection mechanism is capable of identifying the oscillations' magnitude, but not their specific, concatenated patterns. Additionally, this study shows that the model's population data, when analyzed using its normal form, can detect the approach of a major population change, such as a regime shift, but only if this study's specific detection technique is employed. In general, however, the model's population data, when analyzed using its operator theorem-based detection mechanism, can detect the approach of a major population change, such as a regime shift, for a larger class of models, such as those exhibiting a 1-to-2 crossover in their population trajectories. Our analysis uses 18,000 galaxies from the SDSS to assess this effect. To distinguish the impact of the central active nucleus from other non-local starbursts, we compare galaxies with an active nucleus to those without one. Our study uses several characteristics including gas content, metallicity, mass, and the presence of interactions or mergers. Our analysis indicates that galaxies with an active nucleus, regardless of whether they are massive or not, have higher non-local starbursts compared to galaxies without an active nucleus. However, when considering only galaxies with extensive non-local starbursts, those with an active nucleus tend to have lower mass-buildup rates, likely caused by mass loss during major mergers. As a result, galaxies with an active nucleus appear no different from those without one when controlling for non-local starbursts. Our study provides evidence that the mass-star formation rate relation turns over due to increased non-local starbursts during major mergers, leading to additional mass without matching mass-star formation rate increase. Parallel programs can experience faults that require the repair of fences, which establish the dependency order for program instructions, thereby ensuring atomicity and termination for concurrent operations like lock releases and conditional updates. This research focuses on fence repairs using self-downgrade and self-invalidiation, introducing a new "escape hatch" strategy that facilitates repair, and resulting in a linear increase rather than a cubic one for some programs. Some key characteristics of this new approach are outlined, and it is shown that it can result in faster program restarts due to reduced memory validation, but may lead to unanticipated busy-wait cycles during recovery. To address this issue, a new detection method is proposed to identify programs that can benefit from this strategy, resulting in the optimal use of the "escape hatch" approach. Simulation-based testing confirms the effectiveness of this method, resulting in a significant improvement (by a factor of 10) in the time it takes to restore programs. Some well-known programs, including database systems and file systems, can take as little as 20-30 microseconds to be reinitialized. The potential of this approach to be combined with other repair strategies is also discussed, and it is demonstrated that the simplest form of this strategy can be effective, even in the absence of program characteristics. Lastly, a reflection is offered on the implications of this research for the design of program recoveries and the use of program analysis. Furthermore, a distinction is drawn between program behaviors that can benefit from this strategy and those that rely heavily on memory validation, and a new frontier is identified for future research in this domain. Some limitations of this research, including the exclusive focus on the x86-64 processor architecture and the lack of theoretical validation, are also acknowledged. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It is demonstrated that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset |A+B| remains close to 2k. It is shown that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. This improvement builds upon earlier work by Berg'er, Shaltiel, and Sz'ekely, as well as on recent research by Peluse and Prendiville. Key components of the proof rely heavily on an application of the polynomial method and an extension of an additive combinatorial theorem identified by Tamar Zieglert. It is further revealed that this enhanced Freiman's 3k-4 theorem has implications for the bilinear forms problem, in which it yields an alternative proof of a recent result achieved by Berg'er, Shaltiel, and Sz'ekely. Finally, it is demonstrated that this strengthened form of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem can be derived from a simpler conjecture concerning sumsets, which is identified as F(4,2). Consequently, all its implications, including those for the bilinear forms problem, can be established from this simpler framework. In addition, it is demonstrated that this new framework can yield results for cases of larger subsets A and B. X-ray images contain valuable information that can aid healthcare professionals in making informed decisions, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.  By combining computer-technology with clinical expertise, a predictive model can be developed to classify patients who require intensive care unit (ICU) admission based on their X-ray images. To contribute to this goal, this study collects and analyzes a comprehensive set of features related to ICU admission, including developing a user-friendly interface for annotating COVID-19 X-ray images that can be used to identify critical regions. By examining 4482 annotated pixels across 1000 X-ray images, a large dataset of features was extracted using gray-level and texture-based methods. However, our analysis reveals that only a small percentage of these features can distinguish between patients who require ICU admission and those who do not. To address this, a set of top-performing features was identified using a combination of filtering and classification techniques. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the potential effectiveness of computer-aided analysis of X-ray images in identifying critical regions that can aid in classifying patients for ICU admission. Our research is ongoing, and we plan to expand our dataset and incorporate additional features to further validate our approach. Our code is publicly available on GitHub, and we are exploring opportunities for collaboration with healthcare organizations and researchers to accelerate our progress. High-quality X-ray images with precise annotations are crucial for developing accurate computer-aided classification models. To facilitate widespread adoption, we introduce a straightforward annotation scheme that can be applied to chest X-ray images, enabling a wider range of researchers and practitioners to contribute to this goal. By expanding our dataset through a crowd of reliable annotators, we aim to advance the development of computer-aided models that can aid healthcare professionals in identifying critical regions of lung injury from COVID-19. To facilitate the annotation process, we integrate our approach with a user-friendly interface that includes pre-defined labels for easy reference. Our enhanced dataset includes a broader range of features related to ICU admission, including the identification of specific locations within the lung. By extracting a comprehensive set of features using gray-level and texture-based methods, we demonstrate the potential effectiveness of computer-aided analysis of X-ray images in classifying patients for ICU admission. Our analysis highlights the importance of selecting the most informative features, resulting in which our results show significant improvement in classification performance. Ultimately, our research paves the way for the development of advanced computer-aided classification models that can aid healthcare professionals in making informed decisions during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our code is publicly available on GitHub

The universal simplicial collection is a universal construction for functors from the simplicial category to a given category that preserve simplicial identities. It has equivalent forms as both a simplicial object within a specific category and a simplicial set. We argue that if the category in question is suitable, namely groupoids with connections, the universal simplicial collection will itself be a simplicial groupoid with connections. This equivalence leads to an isomorphism between the simplicial set of simplicial groupoids with connections and the category of groupoids with connections, both of which serve as simplical categories. Our proof employs the categorical language of yoneda embedding and natural transformations as functors. Recently, Golay complementary sequences have gained popularity due to their utility in signal processing applications, particularly in sensing scenarios, where they can help reduce interference by utilizing an alternative detection approach, known as energy-based sensing. Building upon this concept, researchers have introduced Golay complementary arrays that offer enhanced performance and a more straightforward implementation process. This work contributes to the field by presenting novel constructions of 6-phase and 8-phase Golay complementary arrays, utilizing a set of binary sequences derived from the Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem code. These creations can be viewed as modifications of the ring excitation strategy, allowing for the inclusion of non-cyclic sequences within the array structures. A numerical evaluation indicates that the newly designed Golay complementary arrays outperform their existing counterparts in terms of spectral nullification and maximum sidelobe level in most cases. Notably, one of the newly designed 6-phase Golay complementary arrays matches the performance of the optimal design, while another outperforms it in spectral nullification but falls short in sidelobe level. Additionally, this work provides an executable MATLAB code for generating these new designs, along with their performance assessments. This code is freely available for download from the open repository, where it can be accessed with the identifier https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.88164. This study demonstrates the superiority of its proposed Golay complementary arrays over the current state-of-the-art options, and it paves the way for further research on non-binary versions of these arrays. Nonetheless, developing an efficient detection approach for these arrays, beyond the energy-based sensing method, remains an unresolved issue and an area worthy of exploration. This work lays the groundwork for investigating new detection strategies in the context of Golay complementary arrays. Lastly, it is worth noting that the code provided in this study can facilitate the design of frequency offset Golay complementary arrays, by utilizing the array's periodic property to transform it into a new design featuring a frequency offset. This capability enables the creation of arrays with a frequency offset by leveraging the code's executable MATLAB code. Moreover, this study demonstrates that executing the code with a machine learning framework, such as TensorFlow, can lead to data storage issues. This problem was addressed by converting the code to an auto-Python script, thereby rectifying the data storage challenge it presented. This study's code, though originally designed for array creation, can also serve as a starting point for developing new detection approaches. It is essential to note that the code provided in this paper can be executed on a regular computer

By utilizing homotopy theory methods, we are able to find a connection between counting subsets and calculating homotopy groups. Every day, individuals suffer from traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), which hinder neural development and disrupt brain function, affecting millions of people worldwide. To enhance TBI rehabilitation, doctors use neurointensive care to minimize further brain damage, but this treatment's success greatly depends on accurately assessing the injured brain area.  However, diagnosing this area is challenging because it relies on comparing a patient's individual brain scans to normal brain development patterns. To achieve this, medical professionals use templates that match the average brain structure, but these templates fall short because every brain is unique. To improve this process, researchers have been using machine learning models, specifically variational auto-encoders (VAEs), to accurately identify the area of brain damage by learning from normal brain development data. These models generate accurate, detailed predictions about the area of damage by learning the normal brain structure's patterns, but they have difficulty dealing with diverse data sets because they only consider the core information. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a progressive Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) that efficiently processes complex data by breaking down brain development into sections, like building blocks, and then using a discriminator to improve the model's performance. By doing this, we can accurately predict the area of brain damage by combining local details into a complete picture. Experimental results show that our progressive VAE model outperforms traditional VAEs when dealing with difficult, challenging data sets because it can handle diverse, hard-to-classify cases just as well as it can easy cases. Furthermore, our model's performance was compared to other machine learning models, and it consistently ranked highest in accuracy and robustness. To validate the model's performance in real-world scenarios, brain damage synthesis examples are provided, and the code is publicly available for easy access. With this model, medical professionals can accurately assess the area of brain damage by comparing a patient's individual brain scans to normally developing brain structures, which can minimize further brain damage and improve TBI rehabilitation. Therefore, we believe integrating this model into clinical practice will lead to better outcomes and faster, more accurate treatment, resulting in peace of mind for both patients and their families. Notably, this phenomenon can be seen in the context of unextendible product bases, a concept previously studied in the context of pure states. Our work expands the understanding of unextendible product bases by identifying instances of nonlocality that are resistant to environmental disruptions in a variety of systems, extending the scope of such bases to encompass mixed-state scenarios. We demonstrate the creation of such robust quantum nonlocality in scenarios involving separate preparations of spin-1/2 particles and in systems based on Bloch vectors. GP 2 is an abstract syntax tree representation of graph programs used for query optimization, and a variety of database systems employ variants of this design. Despite its widespread adoption, the GP 2 framework lacks a publicly accessible compiler that can convert queries into efficient execution plans. To address this gap, we have developed an extended version of the GP 2 compiler, which we call Enhanced GP 2 (EGP 2). This compiler can translate queries into plans for evaluation on graph databases, utilizing a variety of optimization techniques available in modern graph databases. We have also created a web-based tool that allows users to interact with the EGP 2 compiler, providing a user-friendly interface for users to set parameters and observe the generated plans. Our Enhanced GP 2 compiler is an open-source project, and we have included the source code as part of this submission. With EGP 2, we aim to provide a valuable resource for both industry practitioners working on graph databases and academic researchers conducting performance-related evaluations, by making the source code available under the terms of the MIT License. We have incorporated multiple optimization features into the EGP 2 compiler, including distributed processing, by leveraging the Neo4j property-traversal algorithm as its core execution engine. To facilitate communication between the compiler's components, we have established a shared interface called CompGP 2, which we have introduced in this study. Furthermore, we have conducted thorough performance evaluations of the EGP 2 compiler, integrating it with the Neo4j database, and have compared its results with the native Neo4j compiler, demonstrating its effectiveness. We have also created a choice of scenarios for users to select optimization settings, that can be used with the compiler's current version. To accommodate various graph databases, we have designed the compiler as a compiler framework, called the OpenGP 2 compiler, that can be used with different database implementations. We have integrated the OpenGP 2 compiler with the OpenRDF suite of graph databases, and have conducted further performance evaluations with this integrated version, obtaining comparable results with the standalone EGP 2 compiler. We have established a website for the EGP 2 compiler, providing full documentation and a code repository for the project, available at https://github.com/CompGP2/EGP2. We have also created an online tool that allows users to set parameters and observe generated plans, available at http://comp.gp2.compsci.uoa.gr/. Contrary to traditional supervised learning methods, self-supervised learning models train on unlabeled data, leveraging contrastive learning to extract valuable data representations. By exploring various contrastive learning architectures used for feature extraction, including Siamese Networks and the Linear Projection Network, we have identified a uniform framework that integrates these structures. This integrated framework, revealed through a linear decomposition of the projection network, demonstrates equivalent performance to specialized architectures, thereby facilitating the exploration of contrastive learning through a unified framework. This approach holds particular importance for large-scale self-supervised pre-training, as it allows for the fine-tuning of models using an unlimited supply of cheap positive pairs generated from the dataset itself. This enhanced stability, in turn, allows for the exploration of various hyperparameters and different pre-training objectives without risking a deterioration of the model's performance. This knowledge can further be leveraged to inform the design of future self-supervised pre-training methods, aiding in the detection of potential pitfalls and dead-end paths. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, the detector was succeeded by an upgraded variant known as CMS-SI, where the reconstruction of the upgraded forward pixel pilot slices was handled by the University of Auckland in partnership with the University of Adelaide and the University of Auckland's University. This study reviews the modification made to the pilot slice's reconstruction software to match the upgraded detector features. Furthermore, it presents the results obtained from the offline and real-time comparison of data, as well as the associated closed-loop performance. Additionally, it outlines the key challenges encountered and the subsequent software revisions. Finally, it provides an overview of the lessons learned from this experience, which is relevant to the ongoing and future detector upgrades in the CMS system. Co-Imit bypasses the need for expert demonstrations by utilizing agent-to-agent imitation learning between a student agent and a cohort of experienced peers, thereby reducing the requirements for demonstrations. We thoroughly evaluate Co-Imit across multiple scenarios, including multi-agent scenarios, by examining its effectiveness in various settings and its capacity to handle a range of challenges such as diverse peer abilities, partial information issues, and scalability. MongoDB is a widely used, distributed document-oriented NoSQL database that allows for multiple operations to occur within a single transaction. This transactional mechanism is built on top of a transactional coherence protocol, known as the ycsb protocol, which maintains data consistency across transactions. Verifying the correctness of such a protocol in a multi-process system is a complex task due to the interdependence of transactional operations and the underlying protocol's nested nature. In this research, a new method is introduced for formally verifying the ycsb protocol using the Nenyo framework, which combines model checking and SMT solving to validate the protocol's correctness property. An implementation of the ycsb protocol based on MongoDB's source code was created and used for the verification, which showed that the protocol meets the desired property for up to 256 processes. Any increase in the number of processes caused a failure in the verification, indicating the presence of a known issue in MongoDB's transactional coherence. In addition to verifing the ycsb protocol, this research also introduces a new approach for integrating the Nenyo framework with the KLEE symbolic execution tool, which allows for the inclusion of external functions in the protocol implementation. This integration enabled the successful verification of MongoDB's transactional coherence protocol with the assistance of an external function, which would have otherwise been unreachable by the Nenyo framework. The modified Nenyo framework, along with the MongoDB transactional coherence implementation, is available for download and can be used as a reference for the integration of external functions in the Nenyo framework. The challenge of verifying the ycsb protocol has sparked an interest in the research community, which is shown by the positive feedback received from the attendees at the 25th ASPLOS Conference. The possibility of extending the Nenyo framework to handle other NoSQL databases that employ the ycsb protocol has also been explored, which is a potential direction for future research. The use of the Nenyo framework in the verification of MongoDB's transactional coherence protocol has shown that this approach can be an effective solution for the complex challenge of verifying the correctness of NoSQL databases' consistency protocols. The success of this research has also demonstrated the benefit of collaborating with industry partners, which is exemplified by the partnership with the MongoDB company. The exchange of ideas and knowledge between academia and industry has been facilitated by the presence of industry representatives at the 25th ASPLOS Conference, which has created opportunities for further research collaborations. We begin by defining a task that focuses on refining executive function through a rewriting process, leveraging summaries of past experiences to correct perceptions by reevaluating them. This process involves expressing perceptions as sequences of tasks, comparing them to the original task descriptions, and using the similarities to prioritize the reexamination of certain aspects. Our approach uses a combined model that not only generates the task sequences but also evaluates the relevance of the perceptions themselves, ultimately producing a new understanding via a form of self-supervised learning. This leads to the concept of an executive function network, where our model's performance shows a clear distinction from control models and notable improvements with each training cycle. The results of our experiments reveal a notable enhancement in performance, especially in complex tasks, when using a variant of this network that incorporates an additional layer. This variant demonstrates a comparable level of performance to the standard model when trained under the same conditions but with a significantly greater emphasis on minimizing unnecessary reexamination of the perceptions. Furthermore, this variant performs significantly better when trained with a different method that prioritizes high-quality corrections over the quantity of corrected items. This leads to a significant reduction in the number of reexaminations, confirmed by an independent analysis of our data, and results in a substantial decrease in the diversity of the perceptions that the model acts upon. This, in turn, leads to a significant decrease in the model's performance on a subsequent set of test items that are designed to measure its ability to handle diverse situations. This disconnect between in-model measurements and actual performance suggests a limitation that might stem from the model's focus on executive function, specifically a struggle with balancing the variety of perceptions through an over-reliance on the high-quality corrections provided. This finding guides our exploration of a different approach to training the model, incorporating an iterative process similar to that of human executives, with a focus on gradually introducing variety in perceptions and incorporating a form of forgetting mechanism to prevent over-reliance on earlier learned associations. This approach leads to a significant increase in performance and a return to the initial balance between in-model measurements and actual performance, indicating a possibility that the earlier observed disconnect might have been a transient phase. This, however, raises a new question regarding the permanence of this interpretation, to which we respond by presenting additional experimental results that demonstrate the maintained balance even after the model has been retrained from scratch multiple times. This achieved balance is further confirmed by an analysis of the model's weights, and the fact that this model performs comparably to the original variant even when tested in a different setting

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations.  To gain a deeper understanding, we utilize Nuclear forward scattering to investigate the local and average structural dynamics in BFTO at elevated pressures. Our results show that BFTO exhibits unique average structural changes, contrasted with typical average structural changes observed in other Aurivillius compounds, and displays increased local constraints with pressure, which could be attributed to the large size of Bi cations.  Furthermore, we observe a significant decrease in the Fe-Ti correlation distance with increasing pressure, which may result in increased magnetic interactions, and could be responsible for the enhanced magnetism observed in BFTO under pressure.  Interestingly, we find that the Bi large-size effect overrides any potential tensile stress-induced changes, and that the Ti$^{4+}$ 1s-4f transition provides a suitable probe for investigating BFTO under pressure. Our study sheds new light on the structural dynamics of BFTO under pressure, and may facilitate the design of optimized magnetic properties in this and related compounds. Additionally, we believe that our investigation will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussion about structural changes in BFTO, and may also be of interest to researchers working in the bi-layered BCTO, tri-layered BFTTO, and van der Waals layered BFTO, as well as other pressure-susceptible magnetic materials. Our study was conducted at the ID20 beamline of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF), and the results presented have been peer-reviewed and validated.  Our investigation was a collaborative effort involving researchers from the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, the University of Oxford, and the ESRF.  Our study was partially funded by the University of Oxford, and the results obtained have been submitted to the journal Physical Review Materials for peer-review and potential publication.  Our investigation has provided a new perspective on the structural dynamics of BFTO under pressure, and may facilitate the exploration of other pressure-susceptible magnetic materials.  Our study has demonstrated the effectiveness of Nuclear forward scattering in investigating the local and average structural dynamics in BFTO under pressure, and may also be of interest to researchers working in the field of pressure-susceptible magnetic materials.

Hybrid methods can tackle complex planning problems by balancing discrete and continuous stages, but may struggle with accurate error measurement due to mixed representations. In response, this study develops a posteriori error bounds for a wide range of shortest path problems that combine discrete events with continuous motion, subject to certain conditionality. Specifically, such problems occur in free flight trajectory optimization, where the aim is to identify the shortest time to reach a destination within certain velocity constraints. By leveraging a discrete event model and a continuous dynamics model, planners can minimize transit time by predicting arrival times, but this raises difficulties in handling multiple instances due to different error tolerances. To address this limitation, the paper introduces a discrete continuous shortest path problem that can handle any velocity, along with an a posteriori error bound valid across all instances. As a result, this framework enables efficient error comparison across different velocity constraints. Numerical experiments, covering flight trajectories within various regions, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in tight error estimation. Notably, in cases where spatial constraints are relaxed, the method reveals an interesting relationship with dynamic time warping, a technique for aligning continuous signals. By incorporating the planner's tolerance into velocity calculations, the framework provides significant improvement in tight error bounds, especially in larger domains. Finally, the paper highlights potential applications and future directions for this error estimation strategy in the context of free flight trajectory optimization. By utilizing a simple velocity model, the proposed method can be applied to a broader class of discrete continuous shortest path problems, although more sophisticated models may raise different error estimation challenges. As for adapting the framework to handle obstacles, it could be extended to accommodate discrete velocity options, subject to certain feasibility conditions, but this would require careful evaluation of all instances to ensure global optimality. On the other hand, incorporating noisy sensor measurements could be handled through a robust discrete continuous shortest path formulation, but this would introduce new challenges in error bound estimation, especially in response to different velocity constraints. Finally, the paper notes that developing an efficient solver for large scale discrete continuous shortest path problems remains an ongoing research question, especially in the presence of multiple velocity options, but this could be addressed through a hybrid approach combining customized simplex methods with persistent memory, but this would require careful evaluation of all instances to ensure global optimality. On the other hand, incorporating noisy sensor measurements could be handled through a robust discrete continuous shortest path formulation, but this would introduce new challenges in error bound estimation, especially in response to different velocity constraints. Lastly, the paper suggests exploring further applications in the context of free flight trajectory optimization

Researchers studying intense shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both exact and approximate methods. Approximately, they found that for a spherical void of radius $R$ filled with a universe expanding at rate $\theta$, a shock with intensity $\rho$ at radius $R_s$ is described by $\rho \propto (R_s-R)^{-\frac{4}{3}}$ and temperature $\proportional R_s^{-\frac{4}{3}}$. This relationship can also be expressed in terms of the physical density $\rho \proportional (R_s/R)^{4\theta}$. Additionally, they found that for a given $\rho$ and $R$, there is a specific $R_s$ where $\rho$ remains constant across expansion, meaning the shock's density will always be the same regardless of how much the universe expands. Furthermore, when comparing this to observations of superclusters, they found that $\theta$ must be very close to zero, indicating that the universe is nearly flat. Finally, when considering the temperature of the cosmic microwave background, they found that it does not match the universe's expansion rate, suggesting that it may have been quickly cooled by the expansion of a spherical void. This may also explain the universe's current lack of homogeneity. It is also possible that the universe's matter distribution pattern may be described by oscillations in waves, with the size of these oscillations decreasing over time as the universe expands. This would result in different sizes of voids and areas of high density, leading to varying distances where $\rho$ remains constant. This could potentially be tested by observing objects at very large distances. It is also important to note that big bang nucleosynthesis occurs quickly compared to the universe's expansion rate, meaning its process is not affected by the universe's expansion. This could be tested by calculating the mass of baryons in galaxies, which should match the mass of the light elements produced during big bang nucleosynthesis. This new perspective on shock waves in an expanding universe provides a framework for further research into the universe's properties and processes. It also highlights the importance of considering the universe's vast scales and its implications for physical processes at these scales. We derive an explicit formula for these polynomials and verify that they satisfy the Wronskian relationship characteristic of orthogonal polynomials. Furthermore, our findings facilitate the determination of monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with elliptic potentials, which can be reduced to a second-order form. This reduction allows us to establish an integral transformation to obtain monodromy-free Schrödinger operators, which can be expressed in a more manageable form. We also demonstrate that this approach yields periodic potential examples previously identified by Boechat. Our method extends beyond these specific cases, making it a more general and versatile tool for constructing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators. This advancement leverages the properties of the Toda and Volterra systems of differential equations. Our results can also be viewed from the perspective of symplectic matrix operations and the Fourier-Mukai transform in algebraic geometry. This study builds upon prior research by Boechat, Boito, and Freitas, among others, and enriches our understanding of the Toda pair with a 2-to-1 correspondence. Recent studies have highlighted the potential benefits of utilizing degree-degree correlated low-density parity-check (DDC-LDPC) codes to mitigate the adverse effects of binary deletion channels. However, the fundamental performance limitations of DDC-LDPC codes under this interference are not yet fully understood. This work delves into the essential performance characteristics of degree-degree correlated protograph codes when transmitted over a binary deletion channel. By analyzing the scaled minimum distance of these codes, we derive non-asymptotic density power constraints for DDC-PCs, providing a practical limit for their performance. To validate our findings, this work conducts extensive numerical simulations using both custom-designed and randomly generated degree-degree correlated codes, matching our theoretical predictions closely. Furthermore, our results reveal that degree-degree correlation can lead to significant performance gains, with some codes approaching the limit set by the binary erasure channel capacity. To achieve this limit, we develop a new criterion for designing DDC-PCs, focusing on maximizing the largest eigenvalue of the degree-degree correlation matrix. By applying this criterion, we can enhance the scaling exponent of the density power constraint by a factor of approximately two, significantly surpassing the previous limit. However, it is essential to note that this improved performance gain is associated with an increased maximum possible degree, potentially leading to higher encoding complexities. This study proposes a novel concept called Independent Situational Awareness (ISA) for swarms of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles. We argue that ISA is crucial for swarms operating in dynamic environments with multiple objectives, but current approaches to swarm flight fail to account for the natural conflicts that arise when individual vehicles pursue their own objectives. These conflicts hinder the ability of the vehicles to achieve their desired outcomes, ultimately limiting the performance of the swarm as a whole. To illustrate the benefits of ISA, we developed a simple scenario in which a swarm of three vehicles must navigate to reach three destinations while operating in an environment subject to wind influences. Our results show that by incorporating ISA into the vehicles' navigation, we can significantly reduce the time it takes for the swarm to reach its destinations. This improvement, however, comes with an increased communication burden, which must be considered in the design of the vehicles' controllers. Finally, we emphasize the importance of further research into the leader-follower approach and cooperative coordination of swarms to tackle real-world challenges. To this end, we have made our code publicly available for others to build upon.

This extension allows us to demonstrate conditional freeness for a broad category of matrices, specifically those with the spectral radius of one or fewer, except possibly two eigenvalues with a specific ratio. This theoretical advancement has practical applications in the study of free product and Fock-Schweiz constructions. Moreover, we demonstrate that the open type B condition is necessary to ensure conditional freeness, through a counterexample presented in the third section. This counterexample is relevant to but goes beyond hybrid matrices of type B.

This includes identifying the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of an isometry in the closed hyperbolic triangle, as well as the existence or non-existence of Schur matrices within the open type B set.

The test cases for a program's mutations are typically selected randomly, but this method has limitations, especially for complex programs. Our new approach proposes the use of geometric concepts, such as vectors and higher-dimensional spaces, to systematically identify test cases. Each program input can be represented as a point in a higher-dimensional space defined by the program's parameters, with the program's correct behavior defining the boundary between pass and fail results. The test cases for a program are then the hyperplanes that distinguish pass from fail, and we can determine additional test cases by identifying other relevant points in the pass or fail areas. This method can be applied to a variety of programs, including numerical solvers and control systems, and has the benefit of being a one-time setup process that can generate numerous test cases with little computational expense. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic problem, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly positioned scalar field perturbations, overdense spheres with neutrino fluctuations, and black hole mergers. Our results show no difference in the physical properties of spacetime trajectories compared to standard approaches, while significantly improving the computational cost of solving the initial data constraints. This new technique holds the potential to accelerate modern numerical relativity simulations. This work also paves the way for a further optimization of our code that integrates this new method with existing development of numerical relativity simulations. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Nernst effect in certain magnetic materials, particularly those with weak magnetic ordering, have sparked significant interest. This phenomenon, where a long-wavelength heat wave induces a transverse electric current in response to a small magnetic field, is particularly pronounced in materials exhibiting non-trivial topological magnetic textures, such as magnetic skyrmions. Until now, research has primarily focused on the role of magnetic field in driving the anomalous Nernst effect, with a relatively minor opposing influence attributed to the thermal gradient. This study introduces the concept that the thermal gradient can rival the magnetic field in driving the anomalous Nernst effect. Our findings demonstrate that a significant Nernst angle, indicative of the anomalous Nernst effect, can be achieved in Mn$_3$NiN films through temperature gradients. These results indicate that the spin current generated by a temperature gradient can be utilized to control magnetic textures, offering a basis for implementing a thermal-driven anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials. Notably, this mechanism can function independently of any magnetic field, providing a pathway to the realization of a thermal-driven anomalous Nernst effect in films with stable magnetic patterns. Our research also reveals that an in-plane temperature gradient yields a Nernst angle nearly twice as large as an out-of-plane gradient, offering a means to adjust the effect through temperature gradient direction. Furthermore, our experiments and calculations both indicate that the unusual Nernst effect arises as a result of magnetic skyrmion thin films exhibiting a non-trivial topological Hall response. This understanding may facilitate the development of thermally controlled magnetic systems with both local and global regulation. Additionally, this study identifies two applicable pathways that could be adapted for use with other heavy metallic systems, such as those composed of the heavy elements Gd and Au. Recent advances in large-scale online learning and efficient knowledge acquisition have made teacher-student models a popular choice. One significant challenge in the teacher-student framework is modeling multiple instructors, as instructors may label different aspects of the task or provide inaccurate information. To address this issue, we introduce pair-wise incentives in an iterative student-instructor setting to enhance the student's performance. Our proposed framework, PILE, includes a pairwise loss function that allows the student to distinguish between the correct and incorrect labels provided by each instructor. Through experimental evaluations on multiple datasets and tasks, PILE has consistently demonstrated superior or comparable performance to state-of-the-art baselines, often outperforming them significantly. For instance, PILE achieved a 6.3% improvement in the accuracy of the test set on the Split-Char50 dataset and a 1% improvement on the Formance dataset. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghm-2020/PILE. To facilitate future research on multi-instructor learning, we have introduced the Multi-Instructor Learning at Google Colab, an interactive learning environment that enables researchers to manage online learning experiments and instructor labeling efficiently. This Jupyter notebook can be found at https://github.com/ghm-2020/MIL-Google-Colab. Our research demonstrates the potential of the teacher-student framework to model real-world data with various labeling imperfections, and PILE's ensemble ensemble capabilities could benefit applications involving the evaluation of sensitive content, such as hate speech. To further explore the capabilities of PILE, we have applied our method to the classification of balanced datasets. Our results show no significant differences in the performance of PILE on both the training and test sets, indicating that PILE's outcomes are consistent and reliable. Understanding how to tackle society's challenges, from accelerating discovery and innovation to improving national security and daily life, relies on advancing our knowledge of complex materials and processes. However, determining the optimal methods, as well as the best materials and processes, demands extensive exploration across variable parameters, which is a time-consuming and expensive process. Despite the abundance of existing and potential experiments, the analysis of experimental data represents a significant bottleneck, mainly due to the extensive time required for human experts to interpret and make use of the vast amounts of data collected. To accelerate this process, machine learning techniques, such as automated analysis and decision-making tools, become essential tools. By integrating these methods with multiple sources of information and advanced user interfaces, the user experience can be greatly enhanced for both experienced and new users at user facilities, such as national synchrotron light sources. This can result in a more interactive and accelerated data-driven approach to discovering new materials and processes, as well as a more engaging user experience that fosters community growth. This paper will showcase various machine learning methods being utilized at the ALS, such as integrated automation systems for optimizing protein crystal diffraction experiments and characterizing materials using SCIMITAR, a novel high-speed 2D X-ray detector array. It will also highlight various initiatives being implemented to enhance the user experience, speed up data analysis, and provide easy access to machine learning tools and expertise. This will be accomplished through an engaging user interface that integrates multiple data sources, along with advanced machine learning algorithms that can handle complex datasets and streamline decision-making processes. This includes providing straightforward connectivity to popular machine learning libraries, such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, along with widely used data analysis and visualization tools like Matplotlib, PyMOL, and Tableau. This paper will be of interest to any user, either current or prospective, of the ALS or any national user facility. It will be disclosed at the ALS User Meeting on October 5, 2022, and the author is open to receiving feedback and suggestions before the final publication. This work is also being presented at the 2022 NSF/CNS Workshop on Advanced Machine Learning and Experimental Techniques for Materials Science, and the author invites anyone with similar research to share their work during the designated breakout session. This work examines how a temperature anisotropy affects the linearized gyrokinetic equation for geodesic acoustic modes in a tokamak plasma. A normal mode analysis leads to a dispersion relation, and subsequent analysis yields three distinct regime boundaries influenced by temperature anisotropy: a regime where the mode's frequency is independent of mode number, a regime where the mode's frequency is inversely proportional to mode number, and a regime where the mode's frequency is determined by temperature anisotropy and root cause. Linearized gyrokinetic equation solutions provide equivalent results to previous studies on geodesic acoustic modes, and temperature anisotropy may significantly impact mode dynamics. Numerical simulations within a global geometry demonstrate the potential for temperature anisotropy to increase mode amplitude in areas with high electron density. This work is relevant to ongoing and future tokamak experiments that measure geodesic acoustic modes.

When analyzing the performance of quantum annealing, it is assumed that the system's Hamiltonian follows a peptide-like structure, which is classified as stoquastic. However, this study reveals that non-stoquastic Hamiltonians lead to destructive interference during annealing, causing the algorithm to fail. To mitigate this issue, the system is coupled with an environment to introduce a diagonalizing gauge that results in a decoherent Hamiltonian. This transformation converts the system into a random walker, exploiting the geometric phase to achieve successful optimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that actual experimental implementations, such as those employing spin quantum annealing with a decoherent Hamiltonian, perform better than expected, surpassing the annealing completion probability of complex Congressional landscapes by two orders of magnitude. Additionally, we identify the crucial condition that must be met to prevent destructive interference, which results in optimal annealing when the system's minimum and maximum Hamiltonian are anti-hermitian each other. This study provides a new perspective on the issue with non-stoquastic Hamiltonians and presents a groundbreaking solution to this problem. Introduction Quantum annealing (QA) has emerged as a prominent algorithm for addressing complex optimization problems that arise in various fields, such as finance, chemistry, and biology. Despite its promising outcomes, several theoretical issues may impede its success, particularly destructive interference, which can occur when the system's Hamiltonian is non-stoquastic. Notably, for the Drinfeld-Jimbo Toda model, we have established a direct connection between these Ward identities and the Frenkel-Zagier mirror symmetry. As a result, we derive multiple corollaries, including the development of a concrete formula for correlation functions in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model, as well as a demonstration of the relationship between three-dimensional quantum numbers and genus-zero components. Ultimately, this newfound understanding of the Toda model may provide a suitable framework for addressing more complex theories, such as the Toda field theories advocated by Zamolodchikov. Iterative matrix inversion, a fundamental computation in linear algebra, has numerous applications in data analysis and scientific research. While direct inversion is impractical for large datasets, an iterative approach can be feasible. In this study, we build upon the success of [XG] factored iteration, leveraging the capabilities of GPU acceleration, and extend their method to higher order approximation. By deriving a general framework, we demonstrate that our approach yields a linear convergence rate, and through extensive benchmarking, we showcase its superiority over [XG] factored iteration. Furthermore, we incorporate our method into the Python package 'iterative_inversion', making it easily integratable into popular data analysis frameworks like scikit-learn. Critical code segments are also openly contributed to the Python framework 'cublas_pyx', enabling PyPy-based GPU acceleration. Through its implementation, 'iterative_inversion' demonstrates comparable or better performance compared to direct inversion methods on various datasets. In particular, it exhibits enhanced performance when datasets are sparse or have low connectivity, and it successfully completes challenging computations on datasets with up to 128 million samples on a single GPU. The study also explores ways to further improve performance by optimizing memory access patterns and adapting the iteration depth to the specifications of target GPUs. Through its efficient use of GPU memory and potential for significant speedups, 'iterative_inversion' provides a promising pathway for processing large datasets. The study makes the following key contributions to [XG] factored iteration: it achieves a 4-5 times speedup on a V100, a 5-6 times speedup on a K20, and a 7-8 times speedup on a Titan X; it reduces memory usage by a factor of 5 on a V100, a 6 times on a K20, and a 7 times on a Titan X; it completes challenging computations on datasets with up to 128 million samples on a single V100; and it provides the cublas_pyx PyPy-based GPU acceleration package. The authors have also demonstrated that the unified scheme is a robust tool for predicting the form factors of mesons throughout the entire meson spectrum. The results obtained with this approach match the outcomes derived from dispersion relations, and the former are consistent with the data from lattice simulations and quark-model interpretations. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet suspended in an air current under the influence of an electric field, the droplet's behavior remains poorly understood when surrounded by other droplets. This study delves into the previously unexamined realm of this scenario. When the droplet is subjected to a high-frequency electric field in a confined space filled with aerosols, it exhibits a unique characteristic where it maintains a stable temperature across its surface due to the dissipation of electrical energy. Notably, this feature can result in the droplet's ignition in an air current, where the vaporized substance would normally suppress this process. The droplet's ability to manage its surface temperature is reflected in the thermal fluctuations that occur, leading to the situation where another droplet, positioned close to the first, experiences thermal fluctuations caused by the presence of the initial droplet. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies dimensionality reduction to identify low-dimensional equations describing a system's dynamics, we have created two enhanced versions specifically tailored for nonlinear systems. The first version, boundSMLearn, finds the most suitable parameters for a dimensionally reduced model when certain constraints apply. The second version, aggrSMLearn, combines multiple dimensionally reduced models to create a single, unified model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms using examples from environmental science, biology, and physics, significantly speeding up the dimension reduction process by leveraging computational intelligence. Furthermore, we explore how increasing the amount of available data enhances the precision of the dimension reduction, and ultimately the predictive models. Additionally, we explore how different dimension reduction algorithms compare to our proposed methods, and notably, how our proposed methods yield more efficient and precise results when compared to traditional approaches. With the ever-increasing wealth of data being generated from sensors and experiments, our proposed algorithms provide a valuable solution to tackle some of the underlying challenges related to complex system modeling. A novel, self-sustaining wave solution called solitons has been a fundamental phenomenon governing various nonlinear partial differential equations. Solitons possess remarkable properties, including inelastic interactions and the ability to transmit information through amplitude modulation. The discovery of 1-soliton solutions in the Korteweg-de Vries equation marked the beginning of extensive research in this field. However, this equation exhibits a peculiar trait where an incoming soliton is reflected as an outgoing breather instead of another soliton. To address this challenge, numerous approaches have been developed to engineer networks of solitons with specified interaction outcomes. One such method involves introducing a designed component that triggers a self-sustaining, three-soliton configuration through a collision. In this study, our aim is to eliminate the need for pre-designed elements by identifying a natural scenario in which a two-soliton system spontaneously produces a self-sustaining three-soliton state. This remarkable phenomenon arises when two colliding solitons, initially moving in the same direction, undergo a specific phase-lagging interaction. As a result, their combined effort transforms into a stationary two-soliton state, which itself becomes a self-sustaining three-soliton system. We demonstrate that the resulting three-soliton state exhibits a persistent phase-lagging relationship with the original two-soliton state that gave rise to it. To validate our findings, we employ both numerical and analytical approaches in the context of the Ablowitz-Ladik discretized Toda chain. Our study's self-contained, universal implications are applicable to any nonlinear system that can produce long-lived, two-soliton states in a broad range of parameter values. Consequently, we can generate a vast array of self-sustaining, three-soliton states through simple adjustments of these parameters, which are an elementary subset of the intricate component networks that have been engineered in previous studies. Our ground-breaking discovery provides a new, uncomplicated approach for creating a diverse range of self-sustaining, multi-soliton states in complex systems through the deliberate design of a fundamental, two-soliton state. Additionally, our study offers an unprecedented opportunity to examine a natural, three-soliton system resulting from a two-soliton collision in depth, which paves the way for exploring its underlying properties and potential applications in various fields. One such area is the propagation of intense laser light in matter, where our findings could be used to create a self-sustaining, multi-soliton state in plasmas

The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while enhancing the performance of linear and logistic regression inquiries. Key improvements include a 5-6 orders-of-magnitude boost in single-precision arithmetic, a 4-5 times faster execution, and support for non-integral data types. Moreover, SIMC 2.0 achieves a 2-3 times faster encryption process and secures training against manipulation. To illustrate its efficacy, SIMC 2.0 is applied to the secure execution of linear and logistic regression, as well as neural networks on a local network and over the internet. In the last few years, several pharmaceutical companies have invested heavily in pairing existing medications with newly developed ones that can benefit from the interactions of two molecules. This partnership, known as a Drug Pair, has the potential to accelerate healing processes and reduce side effects. By focusing on this opportunity, many organizations are seeking a reliable and efficient method to evaluate the effectiveness of medication pairs. One such approach, widely adopted, involves using relational neural networks to assess pairs based on their individual properties. Although numerous models employing this technique have been proposed in recent years, there is still a lack of clear guidance to follow, primarily because each proposal has introduced its own unique metrics, models, and data sources. To address this issue, our proposed framework provides a comprehensive overview of relational deep learning methods for drug pairing, while also offering distilled knowledge from each individual model. Furthermore, our framework includes a comprehensive benchmark containing 14 state-of-the-art relational model variants, along with their corresponding code, data, and evaluation metrics. By utilizing this benchmark, researchers and practitioners can easily compare the performance of different model variants using identical data and evaluation metrics. Our experimental results reveal that simple baseline models frequently excel in drug pairing tasks, often surpassing the performance of more complex state-of-the-art models. Our study also explores the interaction between model selection and data availability, providing valuable insights that can guide future research in this area. With the continuous growth of bioassay data, our framework is well-positioned to handle larger and more comprehensive datasets, providing a foundation for enhancing the performance of drug pairing models through the incorporation of supplementary bioassay information. By exploring different initialization techniques for the pair scoring task, our work has the potential to contribute meaningfully to the development of relational learning methods. Our framework is publicly available at https://github.com/DrugPairScoring/UnifiedPerspective, inviting anyone to collaborate and co-develop this project. By cooperating, we aim to accelerate progress in drug pairing and make pair scoring more effective. In addition to advancing pair scoring, our study also seeks to facilitate knowledge exchange between the computer-aided drug discovery and pair scoring communities by hosting a knowledge-sharing session at the next Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS). Everyone interested in participating is warmly invited to join us during this session. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders. This research analyzes the impact of mandatory mental health treatment for offenders on the recovery process. By leveraging data from the State of Michigan, specifically court-ordered therapy imposed on convicted individuals, our study aims to investigate this effect. We employ a regression analysis comparing the mental health progression of offenders undergoing required therapy to those who did not receive therapy. The results indicate that court-ordered therapy leads to noticeable improvements in mental health, as measured by the GMHI score, among offenders who were mandated to undergo therapy compared to those who were not required to undergo therapy. Furthermore, this benefit extends to offenders who were sentenced to prison, demonstrating that therapy can be beneficial even in prison settings. When dealing with a mixture model whose components are themselves statistical distributions, the unknown parameters can pose a significant barrier to achieving maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). This study addresses the challenge by introducing a generalized maximum likelihood estimation (GMLE) method, enabling the direct or indirect recovery of the mixture component parameters. This achievement is coupled with a novel result demonstrating that GMLE can be used as a linear transformation of the MLE of the mixture parameters, thereby facilitating the application of classical sampling theory to derive lower bounds on the mean squared error of GMLE estimators. This theoretical advancement holds far-reaching implications, as it implies that the classical results on the efficiency of MLE, along with its second-order asymptotic properties, can be applied to GMLE estimators. This, in turn, paves the way for a more streamlined approach to establishing lower bounds on the mean squared error of GMLE estimators, especially in scenarios involving multiple parameters and large samples. This method is particularly useful for addressing design-related questions, such as the optimal choice of mixing weights. Furthermore, this study provides a GMLE-based framework for establishing lower bounds on the mean squared error of estimators, which can be illustrated through the derivation of a minimum bound on the mean squared error of GMLE estimators for the mean parameter. This study also includes an analysis of the performance of GMLE estimators in the context of sampling from mixtures of discrete and continuous distributions. All the theoretical results are complemented by extensive Monte Carlo simulations, as well as a real-world example, to demonstrate the accuracy of the derived bounds and the superiority of GMLE over the existing methods. This study addresses the challenging issue of estimating mixture component parameters, obtaining consistent estimates, and provides a framework for establishing lower bounds on the mean squared error of estimators, which can be applied across a broad spectrum of statistical applications. Giventhal claims that given any analytic variety $X$, a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ defined on $X$ has a closed range in the set of analytic functions on $X$. We aim to provide a more general proof of this fact by showing that for any analytic variety $X$, a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ defined on $X$ induces a surjective mapping onto the set of analytic functions on $X$ when combined with a linear differential operator $D$ with respect to the space of analytic sections of a torsion-free coherent sheaf on $X$. Notably, this proof holds for differential operators that are not necessarily locally finite, which is a more demanding condition than the one considered by Giventhal. Re-identifying individuals across camera networks without labeled data poses a significant challenge. A common issue with existing methods is the failure to account for the person who is being searched, often referred to as the probe, which can lead to decreased re-identification efficiency. To address this problem, we develop a new large-scale unsupervised re-identification approach, incorporating a distinctive feature of probe images which can help differentiate them from other individuals. By transforming the problem into a classification task where the probe is identified among a mixture of identical twins, we design a contrastive learning-based system to learn the probe's features. This probe-aware model is then used to enhance the re-identification performance for both the probe and non-probe images. Our method produces outstanding results, achieving top ranks in the DukeMTMC and PrID450S benchmark datasets, outperforming the current state-of-the-art techniques by a considerable margin. Our approach also exhibits exceptional classification skills on non-re-identification classification tasks such as animal species classification and flower classification. Our code is available online at our website. This observation gives us an idea to further expand our model's capability to recognize subtle differences between individuals within a single person category by dividing the person dataset by sex. The updated model achieves a higher re-identification accuracy for individuals of the same sex and provides a useful observation on our dataset's distribution. Our model can be trained end-to-end using a single GPU within 24 hours for the Duke dataset, which is a significant improvement over previous methods requiring massive clusters of GPUs and over a week to train. These observables can be used to calculate the pion decay constant at finite volumes, and also determine the quark mass at the next-to-leading order in the chiral perturbation theory. We examine the two-current associations in the pion, and show that they are volume-independent, in contrast to the point-like correlators. Furthermore, we find that the finite volume effects in the three-point correlators can be completely removed by the two-current associations. This implies that if the quark mass is expressed in terms of the pion mass, the finite volume corrections in the two-point point correlator can also be eliminated using the same parameters that describe the three-point correlators. We verify our calculations using an lattice simulation with quark masses that are relevant to the physical world, and the results support our theoretical predictions. Building on the concept of stable K theory by Joyce and Kaad, we establish an equivariant quantum K theory for banner varieties. These varieties, introduced by Amerikoski and Huh, are a class that includes flag varieties, Schubert varieties, and partial flag varieties. We demonstrate the relationship between quantum K theory and Iwahori-Heise Nagaya reciprocity law for banner varieties. Moreover, we derive connections between quantum K theory and quantum cohomology, specifically showing the correspondence functors are compatible with each other. This connection enables us to utilize results from quantum cohomology to study quantum K theory. Lastly, we identify an equivariant version of the GW=K correspondence by Baader and Toda for certain types of banner varieties. These findings collectively contribute to a deeper understanding of quantum K theory for banner varieties and its relationship with other mathematical concepts.

To enhance our model's performance, we incorporate a module responsible for refining the super-edges and another for refining the hyperedges, both of which can be pre-trained in an unsupervised manner. Our method, HyperGraphGuide, takes the form of a two-stage process where we first identify potential super-edges, then construct the hypergraph in the next stage using these covers. We examine temperature and intensity relationships in the photon distribution of thermal atomic samples, determining how interactions between atoms and the semi-classical thermal motion affect these relationships. Our analysis indicates that the correlation between intensity and photon distribution can be controlled through changes in temperature, enabling a precise adjustment of photon statistics to match requirements for various applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate that photon distribution can be accurately modeled using a new semi-classical approach, validated through comparisons with experimental data. This approach facilitates the prediction of necessary experimental conditions to achieve desired photon statistics. In scenarios where large numbers of atoms are involved, we show that the semi-classical thermal motion has a negligible impact, justifying the commonly applied approach of ignoring this effect in such cases. However, for smaller numbers of atoms, our findings highlight the significance of considering the semi-classical thermal motion in order to accurately understand photon distribution and correlation phenomena. Experimental demonstration of these concepts will provide valuable insights into the development of thermal atomic samples with optimized photon statistics. This work is a first step towards a more comprehensive understanding and modeling of thermal atomic samples with low temperatures, a prerequisite for the realization of quantum applications using semi-classical photons.
