We examine the production of binary black hole mergers within the first stars using a one-zone model for gas formation and pollution. By tracking the enrichment of the Early Universe, we focus on the most massive objects: small nuclear star clusters and the Milky Way's early nuclear cluster. For a Hubble constant of 0.069, we find that binary black hole mergers born from first-star matter are dominated by low-mass systems, with a merger rate density of 0.01-0.05 Gpc^-3 yr^-1. However, if we consider nuclear star clusters as the primary sites of binary black hole formation, as suggested by the masses of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, we find a significantly higher merger rate density of 1-10 Gpc^-3 yr^-1, largely consisting of intermediate- to high-mass systems. These predictions contrast significantly with the observed binary black hole merger rate density, with implications for the formation of intermediate- to high-mass black holes in low-metallicity environments. Furthermore, our model forecasts a significant population of binary black hole mergers detectable by LIGO/Virginia Tech's third-generation detectors, particularly in the low-frequency band. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we've observed it can successfully prevent unwanted accelerations during the yellow and red phases. Notably, our study shows that the proposed method excels when there are disruptions in communication between vehicles, specifically when there are losses due to wireless signal interference. Moreover, the results indicate that the proposed method may generate vehicle speeds that exceed what is considered acceptable by some traffic codes, highlighting the diversity in speed standards across different regions. The code used for the simulation is openly accessible on a repository. The evaluation of the proposed method, combined with the connectivity-related aspects, is the focus of our ongoing research. As part of this exploration, we're investigating how to incorporate additional safety concerns and forecasting techniques into the connected vehicle pipeline. Translating this approach into practice is another area of ongoing research for us. Finally, we're exploring different ways to present the predicted driving behavior to the vehicle's human occupants through the in-vehicle interface. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the organization of written text into sections that reflect the progression of the writer's argument. Despite their widespread use, the meanings of these indicators have not been uniformly defined, which creates difficulties in both human and computer-led discussions about text. One of the key challenges in designing effective text analysis algorithms is the varying way discourse markers are used to annotate texts, which also makes it necessary to develop tools that can learn from user feedback to improve their accuracy when identifying the functions of discourse markers. To address these issues, we introduce DiscSense, an innovative tool that allows users to set a specific section of a text and then identifies the discourse markers within that section that indicate the writer's shift in argument. By utilizing both supervised machine learning techniques and a specially designed interface for user feedback, DiscSense can accurately determine the functions of discourse markers present in the specified text section. To test the effectiveness of DiscSense, we conducted a function-annotating task where participants were asked to use the tool to annotate a subset of the Discourse Treebank with Stanford, which showed significant improvements in accuracy when compared to existing annotations. Furthermore, we gathered a new set of annotations for the Semantic Evaluation Corpus, which includes a wide range of discourse functions and is now available for the community. Additionally, DiscSense can also be used as a teaching tool to introduce students to the analysis of written text and the use of machine learning, by guiding them through the annotation process and providing them with insights into the relationships between language, cognition, and computation. By providing an automated method for identifying the functions of discourse markers, we have also opened up new research directions, such as investigating the differences in how people use certain discourse indicators, such as those that express contrast or cause-and-effect relationships, and exploring whether these variations can be captured by a single machine learning model. Another potential research direction is to investigate whether the ability to accurately determine the functions of discourse markers within a specified text section can be applied to other types of text organization tools, such as the identification of entities and relationships in text. To facilitate this line of research, we have made DiscSense available online, along with all the data and the source code used in our experiments, which can be downloaded from our website. By sharing our tool and data with the community, we hope to contribute to the development of more advanced machine learning models that can accurately analyze the complex structures of written language, which will ultimately lead to a better understanding of how people use language to communicate complex ideas

Mobile robots rely heavily on localizing themselves in relation to their environment, and the best approach depends on the specific sensors used. For devices that only have mobile phone cameras and a chip that supports machine learning operations, there is a growing need for methods that can perform real-time, self-contained localization without the need for wireless connectivity. The challenge lies in developing a system that can effectively integrate visual and inertial data to determine a robot's position and orientation. Existing deep learning-based methods often struggle with scaling to a large dataset, have limited capacity to process long sequences, and can't handle missing sensory inputs very well. Furthermore, the majority of VIO systems that use machine learning struggle with initializing and converging to a stable position estimate, often resulting in inaccurate results or getting stuck in local minima. To tackle these issues, we present an innovative External Memory Attention Visual-inertial Odometry system, capable of efficiently processing a mobile robot's visual and inertial data over time, even with varying sequence lengths and missing sensory inputs. By designing a memory-based system that can prioritize crucial information and minimize unnecessary data, our method significantly improves the initialization and convergence of position estimates, resulting in highly accurate results. We compared our system to multiple state-of-the-art VIO and mapping methods on a large dataset, and it outperformed every other deep learning-based VIO system. The code for our EMA-VIO system has been made publicly available on GitHub.

This study employs a motivic perspective to examine curved K-theory, a homotopy theory inspired by Quillen's K-theory design. By integrating algebraic K-theory with the concepts of stable homotopy theory, we investigate a universal property of curved K-theory. Specifically, we identify a two-component multiplicative cofunctor that reflects the properties of curved K-theory. To achieve this, we draw on features from motivic homotopy theory, such as the 0-truncation functor and the motivic image functor, while also developing a range of technical tools. These tools enable us to demonstrate the existence of a universal property for curved K-theory, aligning with our motivic framework. Furthermore, this existence proof yields consequences for sheafed versions of curved K-theory, including correlations with motivic cohomology and Big Witt vectors. These connections hold across the Nisnevich and étale topologies. By extending our findings to the slice filtration, we gain a broader perspective on the relationships between curved K-theory, motivic cohomology, and Big Witt vectors. This extension also facilitates the exploration of Krull-Schmidt equivalences for curved K-theory. Our research introduces the concept of a'motivic stable funtor', establishing its utility through our study of curved K-theory. This leads us to a related conjecture, according to which the A1-localisation of curved K-theory should behave similarly to the localisation of motivic functors. This conjecture, in turn, suggests a link between curved K-theory and the Grothendieck school's ideas on Galois cohomology. Our work also paves the way for potential interactions with homotopy theory driven by Galois cohomology. By integrating our research with the broader homotopy theory community, we aim to contribute to the further development of curved K-theory. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a result, this method can handle configurations where tidal distortion plays a significant role and can handle first-order perturbations in rotational acceleration. This approach also enables direct computation of global quantities via the sum of local properties.

Numerous experiments compare our approach to other strategies, highlighting its superiority over PCA and L1-PCA in cases with outliers and anisotropic data, as well as its preference for balanced recovery of principal components. We will detail an existing reduced order model for monolithic FSI problems and illustrate the development of a new reduced order model for the segmented case. Furthermore, we will compare the efficiency and accuracy of both monolithic and segmented reduced order models, considering both static and dynamic scenarios. All implementations are built on top of the open-source software libraries Ducan and PyFR, and the proposed methods are applied to a specific aircraft model. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and superiority of the RBM when compared to the original finite element method. Additionally, we observe that the monolithic approach yields more consistent results than the segmented approach, primarily due to the reduction of modal plate contributions in the latter. Nonetheless, the segmented approach still proves more efficient than the monolithic approach for the examined aircraft model. To further improve the RBM, we propose increasing the basis functions per DoF from the current 5 to 10, which results in a marked improvement, albeit from a relatively high baseline. For an agent to successfully explore an unknown environment, having a topological map is crucial. Current methods that extend traditional local navigation systems are key-based approaches, minimalistic representations, or complex metric maps. Key-based methods can struggle with scalability due to their extensive reliance on key storage and matching, whereas complex metric maps often result in impractically high computation costs for optimization-based control systems. In contrast, a new simple yet effective key-free system is introduced, utilizing a HiTMap, a hierarchical topological diagram representation. HiTMap employs an abstract representation of sub-spaces to guide its navigation, with each sub-space identified by a target region within the global coordinate system. The boundaries between these regions are detected using a simple detection algorithm based on the agent's observations, without the need for communication with a parent node. As the agent moves, its region assignments may change due to crossing into a new sub-space, resulting in potential inefficiencies. To mitigate this, an optimized motion planner is developed to prioritize entries that minimize the agent's computation time, reducing the frequency of unscheduled sub-space crossings. The proposed HiTMap system is thoroughly tested in realistic simulations using a 2D autonomous vehicle, demonstrating its capacity to efficiently navigate through an ever-expanding environment, comparing favorably to a leading key-based system. The results show the HiTMap system achieves a 5-7 times increase in exploration speed and a 3-4 times decrease in computation time per time step. The code for the HiTMap project is openly available, along with the developed models and simulation tools. The proposed system provides a promising solution for navigating through an unknown environment using a key-free, hierarchical topological map. The integration of the HiTMap system into an autonomous vehicle is a viable approach for expanding the system's knowledge of the environment, obtaining a significant increase in exploration speed and a substantial decrease in computation time per time step. The current development of the HiTMap project has focused on a 2D autonomous vehicle, presenting an opportunity for future work to integrate the system into a 3D vehicle, as well as exploring new detection algorithms and optimized motion planners. The simplicity and flexibility of the HiTMap system make it a suitable candidate for integrating various sensors and navigation systems, providing a potential platform for developing more advanced artificial intelligence algorithms. This limitation forces programmers to resort to flat indexing methods despite the inherent efficiency of object-oriented programming. We present DynaSOAr, a novel object allocator designed for object-based programming on SIMD devices. It offers a unique blend of static and dynamic memory allocation features, coupled with a memory access pattern that minimizes conflicts and cache misses. Furthermore, DynaSOAr provides a flexible object layout, allowing for object inheritance and polymorphism. Our evaluation reveals that DynaSOAr yields substantial performance gains, up to 7 times, over existing methods. It also demonstrates ease of use and improved code readability by comparing benchmark results with the optimized versions of popular open-source benchmarks. DynaSOAr is an open-source project that can be utilized with various programming languages, including C, C++, and Fortran, and is compatible with a wide range of GPU architectures. Its effective memory management and efficient memory access pattern provide a reliable foundation for developing high-performance object-based programs on SIMD devices. This research is an extension of our previous work on SOAr, an static object allocator, by introducing a dynamic object allocator and achieving even greater memory allocation efficiency. This advancement results in a 5 times improvement in memory allocation speed, a 5 times faster object creation time, and a 3 times faster array construction time. With this improved performance, DynaSOAr can handle larger objects, leading to a potential 5 times better cache locality and further 2 to 3 times better performance. Three-dimensional (3D) tomographic reconstructions of high-altitude clouds have not been achievable with ground-based observations due to their opacity. This study presents a novel approach using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite platforms to create such reconstructions. By taking advantage of the unique viewing perspectives of the MISR satellite, our method utilizes the varying levels of absorption as it observes clouds from different angles. This is demonstrated with an example analysis of a large stratocumulus cloud layer over the Pacific Ocean during the AERIUS campaign, showing that cloud tomography is feasible with the appropriate preprocessing of MODIS data and proper selection of analysis regions. Notably, the results indicate that clouds with a high albedo (reflectivity) Al > 0.25 can be effectively reconstructed, while those with lower albedo may require the use of forward modeling to accurately interpret. The findings of this study have implications for the development of cloud tomography using future satellite missions such as POLDAR. The code and data used in this study are made publicly available to facilitate the development of cloud tomography techniques. We present the discovery of the TOI-712 system, featuring three mini-Neptunes orbiting an G2V star with a high level of activity. The two larger planets, with radii of 2.13 $R_{\earth}$ and 2.28 $R_{\earth}$, have close separations of 3.3 and 6.7 Earth days from their star. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen doped rutile TiO2.  To accurately account for doped p-electrons, we used a GGA+U hybrid method which combines the Ti 3s, 3p, O 2s, 2p states within the DFT framework while employing the Fermi-Dirac statistic.  Our results show that doped p-elements occupy the A-sites in rutile TiO2 structure.  We observed an increase in bandgap energy upon substitution, with a significant shift in energy when the doped p-element is located near the surface.  The energy of doped TiO2 is lowered by 2 eV due to localized state formation, making it less suitable for solar cell applications.  On the other hand, nitrogen doping results in ferromagnetic behavior, while carbon doping leads to antiferromagnetic behavior.  We also analyzed the geometric parameters of doped TiO2, observing a significant expansion of the doped p-element atom and a slight contraction of the surrounding O Ti p-orbital.  We discuss how these results can impact the design of solar cell devices.  Overall, our results indicate that nitrogen doping produces a suitable electronic and magnetic framework for solar cell applications over carbon doping.  We propose the use of nitrogen-doped TiO2 as a surface layer in solar cell devices to achieve optimal energy storage.  Conversely, carbon-doped TiO2 may be more applicable to magnetic storage devices. We compare two different noise impacts: the first originates from the montenaro-roberts-gerald qutrit gate, characterized by its non-kraus form, resulting in an average gate error that scales with the square of the number of qubits; the second, originating from the application of single-qubit pauli channels, results in a gate error that remains constant, independent of the number of qubits. Notably, the montenaro-roberts-gerald noise exhibits a more significant error propagation when combining systems, while the pauli channel noise demonstrates a more manageable error when systems are merged, indicating a potential advantage of using this type of noise in quantum simulations. We utilize the montenaro-roberts-gerald noise to predict error thresholds for the convergence of volume phases, discovering that qutrit gates must operate error-free below a specific tolerance level, regardless of the number of qubits, while pauli channel noise allows for slightly higher tolerance levels. We observe that increasing the number of qubits reduces the efficiency of volume phase convergence, with a significant error propagation when combining systems, while pauli channel noise permits the realization of volume phase convergence with a certain level of gate error, particularly with small systems, further highlighting the importance of selecting the most suitable noise model for quantum simulations. The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter is varied, often in a way that simplifies the problem. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that emphasizes the resemblance between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then show that by applying this approach, we can utilize established numerical methods in computational fluid dynamics to efficiently solve the flow equations. This methodology bypasses the need for precise initial conditions and instead relies on the inherent properties of the system to provide insights, which is particularly beneficial in the context of quantum field theories where initial conditions are generally unknown. When given a set of words, it uses a neural network to generate a melody and a syllable-based neural network to generate a voice to go along with the music. By testing our system on a large dataset of Austrian folk song lyrics, we found that it can produce a reasonable amount of music, even if it's not perfect. Our automated music-making system has the potential to revolutionize the music industry and make music accessible to everyone. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many decades. To shine light on this enigma, researchers are searching for correlations between high-energy neutrinos and UHECRs. By examining 1132 days of data from the ANTARES and IceCube neutrino detectors, this study seeks to explore local connections between neutrino sources and UHECR arrival directions. Although no significant links were initially found, a striking association emerged between four UHECR sources and neutrino directions within a 3-degree radius - with an significance of $4.3\sigma$ - providing a potential pathway to identifying the sources of UHECRs. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that hadronic cosmic rays can be used as messengers to detect and study neutrino sources, or as independent probes of the universe. By examining various neutrino flux predictions, the researchers found that the most stringent constraints on hadronic interactions are obtained for sources with energies in the range of $10^{9.5}$ to $10^{10.5}$. This analysis also highlights that UHECR-neutrino connections can be validated using UHECR octant analysis, resulting in a similar significance of $4.1\sigma$. Lastly, the study shows that the most prominent association holds when considering only the most energetic UHECR events, with an significance of $3.1\sigma$. This finding may be used as a target for future multi-messenger studies using real-time UHECR detection, along with a more in-depth analysis of the data presented here. By doing so, it is possible to determine whether the sources of high-energy neutrons and UHECRs overlap, or if they differ. This study paves the way for such a validation and a more in-depth analysis of the data, along with a review of the methods employed. This review includes updating the data to account for the recently upgraded IceCube detector size, as well as re-examining the results with UHECR sources that consider hadronic interactions in line with the recent findings from the Earth's passage through the galactic cosmic ray spectrum. In educational settings, curiosity is both a driver of personal growth and a key to effective learning, but it requires cultivation to avoid natural declines over time.  By developing a multifaceted measure of curiosity through the combination of physiological signals and self-reported thoughts and feelings, this research explores how primary school students' curiosity evolves over the course of a week-long science learning program.  Initially, results indicate that participants' curiosity levels remain consistent throughout the program, but a more in-depth analysis reveals significant variations in curiosity levels across different days, with certain days exhibiting increased curiosity.  Additionally, the research identifies several key factors that influence students' curiosity, including intrinsic motivation, self-confidence, and interest in the learning activity, as well as various contextual elements such as the learning environment and social interactions with peers and instructors.  Furthermore, the study identifies distinct curiosity patterns in boys and girls, with girls exhibiting higher curiosity levels and a greater desire to learn from peers, while boys demonstrate a greater desire to learn from the instructor and the learning environment.  Finally, the research establishes the presence of individual-specific curiosity dynamics across the program, with certain students exhibiting consistent curiosity levels, while others exhibit more variable curiosity levels that are significantly affected by the learning environment and social interactions. This work introduces a new dimension-free technique for in-depth data analysis, specifically tailored to handle multivariate functional data within any-dimensional domain. Our approach, termed Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Examination (MFSE), builds upon the established singular spectrum analysis framework, accommodating datasets defined on parametric domains such as time series, image spectra, or multi-variable function data. By exploring and identifying patterns in the singular spectrum of the double Hilbert space representation of multivariate functional data, MFSE delivers a comprehensive and transparent approach to discovering hidden structures, dimension reduction, and component identification, facilitated by the exploration tool SE-rot (SE-rotator). Through rigorous theoretical analysis and practical applications, we demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of MFSE in multivariate functional data analysis. Notably, this work also addresses dimension-related challenges in machine learning, encompassing dimension reduction, feature extraction, and embedding, by leveraging the singular value decomposition (SVD) and SE-rot rotators. The proposed framework, along with its implementations and results, is made available through the Rfssa R package, providing a free resource for reproducing our findings and guiding other researchers in applying MFSE to their multivariate functional data. By showcasing its utility on real-world datasets, including atmospheric CO2 concentration data, stock price trajectories, and brain connectivity maps, our work paves the way for MFSE to become a trusted method in the statistical analysis community. The accompanying supplementary materials provide step-by-step reproduction guides for the presented figures and results. The recently developed Rfssa R package, available at https://cran.r-project.org/package=Rfssa, offers enhanced functionality for the proposed MFSE approach. A connected graph G is classified as having a hamiltonian path if there exists a path that visits every vertex exactly once. The smallest number required to achieve this is known as the graph's hamiltonian path index (hpi). We offer a definition for a repeated line graph (RLLG) as G^{\~{}l} such that for each x in V(G), the set of x's neighbors in G is exactly the set of y's in V(G). With this in mind, our main contribution is to prove that an RLLG with an index of 2 is itself hamiltonian. Furthermore, we establish that the property of having an index of 2 is monotone with respect to line graph transformations. Consequently, we are able to demonstrate that the class of RLLGs is equivalent to the class of graphs with an index of 2, and as a result of this, we are able to conclude that it is NP-complete to determine whether an RLLG has an index of 2. Additionally, we provide a definition for a double line graph (DLG) as G^{\~{}2} such that for each x in V(G), the set of x's neighbors in G is exactly the set of y's in V(G). With this in mind, our secondary contribution is to prove that a DLG with an index of 2 is itself hamiltonian. Furthermore, we establish that the property of having an index of 2 is monotone with respect to double line graph transformations. Consequently, we are able to demonstrate that the class of DLGs is equivalent to the class of graphs with an index of 2, and as a result of this, we are able to conclude that it is NP-complete to determine whether an DLG has an index of 2. Building on this, our tertiary contribution is to define that a connected graph G is traceable if there exists a path that visits every vertex exactly once, and if this path's two endpoints can be either connected by an edge, or if there is an edge connecting two vertices of the graph's components after the path's construction. We then establish that a connected graph G^{\~{}l} with an index of 2 is hamiltonian, and we demonstrate this by examining the possible configurations of a 2-indexed connected graph. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  SARS-CoV-2 induces pyroptosis by activating the NLRP3 inflammasome, which is mediated by the caspase-8 and caspase-1 pathways. Our model aims to analyze the dynamics of this process and assess the impact of anti-inflammatory treatments on pyroptotic cell death. 

In our model, we represent an infected cell as a system of ordinary differential equations that capture the dynamics of the NLRP3 inflammasome, pyroptotic cell death, and the activity of cytokines. Specifically, we consider a model that includes an infectious agent $x$ that replicates and interacts with the host, and a model that includes the agent's release and the resulting cytokine levels.

We examine two treatment scenarios in our model: one that reduces the host's vulnerability to infection, and another that inhibits the caspase-1 pathway. Our analysis of the models reveals the conditions under which they exhibit stable equilibrium points, as well as the potential for them to model oscillatory cytokine levels observed in patients with COVID-19. Furthermore, we assess the effectiveness of the two treatment strategies and our results suggest that both can delay pyroptotic cell death and reduce cytokine levels. Our models provide a framework for understanding the complex dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 induced pyroptosis and the effects of anti-inflammatory treatments, and they highlight the importance of considering individual cell responses in host-pathogen interactions. 

In the discussion section, we explore the implications of our model for the implementation of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) prevention strategies and we outline a potential pathway for validating the model against in vitro experiments.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized as the presence of an 'exogenous' state or reward function, which is statistically identified using a non-parametric measurement that assesses the degree of unpredictability present in the reward signal. Subsequent removal of the exogenous state or reward component is achieved through reinforcement learning by increasing the unpredictability of the reward signal, resulting in improved performance when applying this method to multiple scenarios. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that fully eliminating the exogenous state or reward component may not always be possible if it is masked by the agent's inherent noise, thereby compromising the efficacy of this approach. As a complementary aspect, the analysis is coupled with an exploration of the suitability of Biologically Plausible Reinforcement Learning as a method to accomplish this task. Results obtained suggest that this technique can yield successful outcomes, especially in situations where the exogenous state or reward component possesses a simple structure. However, it falls short in cases where the underlying structure of the exogenous state or reward component is complex, necessitating further investigation into this topic. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for tools that guarantee the precision of these programs. To address this need, our project HELMHOLTZ has been developed to provide a sophisticated type-based validation tool for Tezos smart contracts using the OCaml programming language. By incorporating a range of advanced type refinement techniques, HELMHOLTZ elevates the reliability of smart contracts built with refined types, thereby reducing the necessity for repeated testing and re-deployment caused by type errors. Furthermore, to facilitate the evaluation of its effectiveness, a demonstration refinement example for housing rental management is included with HELMHOLTZ, also made available for public review on its official repository on GitHub. Large-scale refinements developed by independent third-party contractors can be tried out using a pre-configured Docker container provided with the repository. By utilizing refined types, developers of smart contracts can enhance their reliability and overall performance, thus making the deployment of these contracts more efficient and less prone to errors. A key method in this area, the unsupervised restoration process using CycleGAN, has demonstrated great promise. However, the primary challenge lies in optimizing the training process, a problem compounded by the necessity to repeatedly train new models for various CT doses. To address this issue, this paper introduces an innovative strategy based on an adaptive instance normalization layer, allowing CycleGAN to restore low-dose CT images across a wide range of doses with minimal training. Experiments conducted on a group of phantom models and clinical images showed that the proposed AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN achieved superior restoration results, with a notable reduction in training losses and artifacts. Compared to conventional methods, AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN demonstrated a remarkable 9 times improvement in PSNR and 19 times improvement in SSIM on average. The code for this project has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zwang86/AdaIN-SCGAN. Furthermore, the field of low-dose CT image enhancement is being opened up for further research and the proposed AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN model is available for testing against various datasets. In terms of potential applications, this technology could be utilized in clinical settings with limited dose capabilities, particularly in pediatric and high-risk patient imaging. The name of the dataset used in this research is "Low-dose CT with 32x32 pixels", and it contains 1000 phantom models with varying levels of noise and 200 clinical images. The dataset can be downloaded from the mentioned GitHub repository. The parameters for the deep learning network were as follows: number of channels = 64, number of channels in the discriminator = 32, number of cycles = 5000, and the lambda values for cycle and identity losses were both set to 10. However, instead of directly finding the mean, some approaches prioritize identifying the mode of a conditional probability distribution function, specifically using conditional neural networks, such as conditional generative adversarial networks (CGAN). Graph neural networks (GNNs) have excelled in various social and engineering tasks by leveraging graph representations. However, GNNs are designed to operate on undirected graphs, which can lead to inaccuracies when working with directed graphs, particularly those representing information flows. Current directional GNN models often rely on modifying existing GNN layers to accommodate directionality, which isn't a comprehensive solution. Instead of a patchwork approach, our novel directional GNN framework LorGN is a thorough and systematic model for processing directed graphs. We introduce a novel directional message passer layer and a new layer that combines information from the directionality-aware predecessor and a specified sub-set of predecessors. Experiments demonstrate that LorGN outperforms existing GNN models and showcases its versatility by successfully being applied to both self-learned and pre-trained settings, yielding superior performance on benchmark datasets. The project's code is now available on the GitHub platform. The paper further explores the integration of LorGN and a state-of-the-art encoder-decoder model, transforming the directional graph classification into a sequential prediction task, which results in notable improvements in classification accuracy. The paper is a candidate for best paper award at ICLR 2022. The paper introduces an open challenge for identifying a directed graph kernel through a proposed neural director mask objective function, which aims to enhance generalisability, before experimenting with a novel application of directional GNNs on temporal graph classification, introducing a new temporal graph generator model, and successfully extending the model to a neural director for temporal graph translation. The paper is a finalist for the ICLR 2022 best paper award. The model's code is available on GitHub. The paper proposes a novel application of directional GNNs to sequential text classification, successfully translating temporal graphs to sequential texts, releasing the model's code on GitHub, and submitting the paper for consideration to NIPS 2022. The paper introduces a novel application of directional GNNs to machine translation, accurately translating technical graphs to technical texts, and makes the model's code available on GitHub. The paper further explores the integration of directional graph elements and a state-of-the-art encoder-decoder model for graph-to-text translation, experimenting with a novel application of directional GNNs to multilingual machine translation, successfully extending the model to directional GNNs with pre-normalised 2-layer embeddings, and releasing the model's code on GitHub. We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to databases represented as relational algebra with the addition of an 'entity' operator. The entity operator, available in some database systems, allows for the retrieval of sets of tuples, in contrast to the point operator used in modal logic which targets individual elements. With the entity operator added to modal $\mu$-calculus, we explore its behavioral equivalence with point operators by developing a point-to-set translation. This translation maintains the original formula's intended meaning, thus providing a basis for the mu-calculus with entity operators to mimic the properties of mu-calculus with point operators. Moreover, this point-to-set translation is applicable across multiple variants of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically with respect to its core operations. On the other hand, we demonstrate that the addition of the entity operator to modal $\mu$-calculus surpasses the expressive power of modal $\mu$-calculus with point operators, mainly due to the entity operator's ability to embed modal $\mu$-calculus within itself. Finally, we investigate the connection between the entity operator and the 'do not know' modality, revealing that the latter can be represented using the entity operator with recursion. This representation, however, requires the ability to refer to the operator's arguments in a recursive manner, an ability that may not be universally achievable. As such, we establish that the combination of the entity operator and basic recursion is equivalent to the expressiveness of first-order logic. This equivalence serves as the foundation for our results with the vectorial extension of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically showing that with the entity operator and basic recursion, the resulting system is behaviorally equivalent to fixed points with an infinite number of arguments. This in turn enables us to prove that with the entity operator and basic recursion, the point-to-set translation can be achieved with a limit of two point operators, or 'arguments', in the mu-calculus with point operators. This, in turn, allows us to derive the same outcomes with the vectorial extension of modal $\mu$-calculus as we have with its scalar counterpart. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves assessing features like size, shape, and the presence/absence of specific patterns, which can be determined through a comprehensive examination of histopathological images. Recent advancements in computational image analysis have paved the way for developing efficient and cost-effective characterization methods, aided by deep learning technology and specially curated datasets. However, a fundamental obstacle in this field is the scarcity of large, high-quality annotated datasets containing a variety of colorectal polyp samples, which hinders development and subsequent utilization of deep learning-based characterization tools in clinical settings. To bridge this gap, our research team has created UniToPatho, an extensive collection of annotated H&E stained images representing different types and stages of colorectal polyps, which can serve as a standard for evaluating and comparing state-of-the-art characterization algorithms. UniToPatho not only supplies a substantial dataset for classifying polyps as adenomas or carcinomas (with a total of 4,851 whole-slide images) but also provides a detailed set of annotations for evaluating abnormality grades in adenomas, based on the Hamburger classification system. To facilitate easy access and utilization of this dataset in computational analysis, our research team has established a clear guideline on the suitable color normalization, pre-processing techniques, and compatible deep learning models. By utilizing UniToPatho, our results demonstrate considerable potential in deep learning-based characterization, with an overall classification accuracy of 94.15% and grade evaluation accuracy of 65.19%, respectively. To contribute further to the development of computational analysis in this field, our research team warmly invites other researchers to collaborate and share their expertise. UniToPatho is an open-source, publicly accessible dataset available at https://github.com/bragagnoloj/UniToPatho, specifically designed to support researchers in developing high-performance computational analysis tools for colorectal polyp characterization. By integrating these tools into clinical workflows, we aim to enhance accuracy, efficiency, and reliability in clinical diagnosis. In addition, our research team has created a user-friendly web application for visualizing and exploring the dataset, along with detailed documentation on dataset creation and characterization results, available at https://unito.patho.iti.unige.ch. By collaborating and sharing knowledge, we hope to establish a robust foundation for developing accurate computational analysis tools in colorectal polyp characterization, ultimately contributing to better patient outcomes. Isotopic analysis indicates an average 17.2 permil delta seventeen value for water in Benenitra chondrites and chondritic particles, and a significantly higher value of twenty permil for water in Chelyabinsk chondrites and chondritic particles. Using the F-batch algebra method, we find exact form factors for higher-spin XXZ chain models. The form factors are obtained from a supertransfer matrix that represents the one-body density matrix and can be used to derive correlation functions. The method employs the affine quantum-group symmetry, specifically $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, to obtain the form factors. Notably, this approach yields a closed-expression for the form factors, enabling the derivation of correlation functions through the quantum-group Casimir operator. The method can be extended to other integrable models, such as the XX+XXZ and XYZ chains, by applying suitable limits. The closed-expression for the form factors provides a valuable tool for verifying lattice versions of bulk observables' correlations and for testing conjectured formulas. The method can also be used to study magnetic form factors and two-body form factors, which involve more intricate calculations. The case study of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain has verified previous findings, while the method has also been used to derive closed-expression form factors for the spin-1 XXZ chain, demonstrating the method's applicability to higher spins. The work presents the affine quantum-group symmetry's role in deriving form factors, which can be seen as stochastic versions of bulk observables' correlations. The method has been made publicly available through the form factors online database, providing accessible code for the calculation of specific models' form factors. The database features a user-friendly interface and detailed instructions on the used notation, ensuring the reproducibility of results. The work has been further supplemented by the creation of the quantum-group tools package, featuring high-performance lattice-site calculation code, specifically designed for the treatment of affine quantum groups within F-batch algebra. The package introduces the QGTensor4j library, which provides affine quantum-group operators and used F-batch algebra symbols, while the parent company, JQuantum, hosts open-source code based on the maintained Git repositories. Speech-to-speech translation, a highly anticipated technology, has significant potential to break language barriers by enabling people to communicate verbally and have translations applied as needed. While significant progress is being made in the field, the current requirement that both the source and target languages be known during training presents a significant hurdle. This requirement not only restricts the scalability of the technology but also limits its effectiveness in the real world due to the numerous possible language combinations that need to be accommodated. This paper explores a breakthrough technique, where translations can be performed without any knowledge of the source language being known, achieved by utilizing a mixture model of multiple parallel datasets to create a single generalized model that can perform translations into a target language without any knowledge of the source language. This model is then used to initiate a cycle of refinement, first using a comparison of the model's predictions to the actual results for a specific source-target language pair, followed by generalizations to all possible target languages. This process results in a final model that can perform zero-shot translations for any given source and target languages. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the translation of speech segments using the GLUE dataset, producing speech samples that are then assessed for their accuracy by listeners, and comparing the results to both machine-based assessments and a widely used machine translation framework. The analysis shows significant improvements in both listener and machine-based evaluations over the current state-of-the-art techniques. The authors further investigate the impact of various factors on the performance of the model, including the number of parallel datasets, the size of the training datasets, and the complexity of the languages involved, providing valuable insights that can inform the design of more effective speech-to-speech translation systems. The authors have generously shared their models and code with the community, marking a significant step towards open research practices. The excellent performance of this approach, coupled with its practical applications, makes it an extremely appealing technique for both speech-to-speech translation and natural language generation. The technique has the potential to be applied to various other applications that involve zero-shot translations, such as generating product reviews for businesses that operate globally. The authors explore the application of this technique to both speech-to-speech and text-to-speech translations, highlighting its immense value in enabling people to communicate more effectively across linguistic boundaries. The groundbreaking nature of this research marks an important milestone in the advancement of speech-to-speech translation technology, paving the way for the development of more sophisticated translation systems that can handle any language pair. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our analysis reveals that the choice of multipoles significantly affects the accuracy of optical force calculations, with the simplest method yielding the largest errors. Notably, even the most advanced methods fail to capture precise insights when the particle size is not commensurate with the wavelength, resulting in force calculations that are poorly defined and erratic in such cases. Consequently, it is essential to select methods that provide a precise description of particle behavior, as the optical force's dependence on wavelength can be very sensitive. Furthermore, we observe that the commonly employed long wavelength approximation, which assumes that electromagnetic scattering behaves like dipolar, falls short of accurately capturing the optical force's variation with the concentration of particles. This shortcoming underscores the importance of employing a more nuanced method that considers the complex interplay between particle size, composition, and the surrounding medium. Our analysis also highlights that accurately modeling the optical force necessitates a precise description of the multipoles, which in turn demands a thorough understanding of the underlying physics. This knowledge should be applicable to an even broader scope of electromagnetic phenomena, encompassing any system where the multipoles are responsible for scattering and force computations. In the context of semiconductor particles, we identify an additional consideration, namely the need to incorporate van der Waals interactions that significantly impact the optical force's accuracy. This complication raises the question of whether it might be possible to devise a general strategy that could accurately model this interaction, thereby further advancing our understanding of the complex electromagnetic phenomena at play. This knowledge could, in turn, be utilized to develop a general approach for tackling a wide range of challenging problems that arise when computing the optical force's behavior. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling on Gd ions within a cubic lattice. By investigating the variation in energy and symmetry of the electrons as the spin-orbit coupling changes, we can see that there is a significant mixing of the t2g and eg orbitals when the spin-orbit coupling is high. This mixing causes a decrease in the energy difference between the top and bottom bands, leading to an increase in the density of states at the Fermi level, a shift in the momentum of the fermi level, and a change in the Fermi surface from semi-circular to elliptical. This breakdown can result in the shifting of charge transfer peaks in spectra obtained from spectroscopic measurements. Our findings may provide a theoretical explanation for the mixed t2g-eig states observed in spectra from some transition metal oxide compounds. Additionally, this concept might be applicable to other systems where there are heavy ions with large bandwidths, and our results also suggest a way to control the Fermi level surface by adjusting the spin-orbit coupling in these systems. This could potentially switch a system from being half-filled to overlapping bands, or vice versa. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in medical imaging has emerged, namely medical imaging editing. This research employs a generative adversarial network to enhance chest X-rays, with the primary goal of creating a more accurate diagnosis through enhanced image quality. Since real-time retouching of chest X-rays is impractical due to exposure control, the editing process focuses on correcting poor exposure, which is a major factor in misdiagnosis. By training a generative adversarial network on a large, diverse dataset consisting of underexposed chest X-rays and their well-exposed counterparts, the model is able to rectify poorly exposed images by comparing them to a dataset of correctly exposed images. With the exception of super-resolution techniques, this study's results indicate that generative adversarial networks outperform other image-to-image translation methods. Moreover, clinical specialists' ratings confirm that edited images with proper exposure more accurately reflect actual conditions. In addition to achieving comparable performance to expert retouching, this research also demonstrates the versatility of medical imaging editing techniques. As a relatively new approach in medical imaging, this study marks the beginning of a broader exploration of medical imaging editing enabled by deep learning. With potential applications in various medical imaging modalities, such as X-rays, ultrasound, and MRI, a significant aspect to consider goes beyond mere diagnosis, also taking into account the perspectives of patients, who view medical imaging as more than just a tool for medical professionals. With this in mind, this study and its findings lay the groundwork for a broader investigation into the realm of medical imaging editing. As a key aspect, researchers should give due consideration to issues of data privacy and ethics in addition to more substantive matters of diagnosis. With appropriate attention to these ethics, medical imaging editing enabled by deep learning is poised to empower patients with a level of control over their medical images, in turn fostering trust and cooperation with medical professionals. Furthermore, this study also demonstrates the capacity of medical imaging editing to address a wide range of medical issues, such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, genetic disorders, mental health, and neurological disorders, by providing a means to accurately and reliably rectify poor quality medical images, thereby facilitating more effective diagnosis and treatment. With this in mind, this study proposes a framework for a user-friendly, intuitive, and interactive medical imaging editing platform that empowers patients to manage their own medical images, addresses a broad range of medical issues, and unlocks the full potential of medical imaging editing enabled by deep learning. We introduce a new, high-performance method for evaluating Newtonian potentials in two-dimensional domains. Our main achievement is a novel, analytically derived formula for the potential values at nodes, enabling simple and efficient implementation of boundary integral methods for solving the Laplace and Helmholtz equations numerically. Specifically, we provide a straightforward way to compute potential values using a highly optimized set of operations on node interactions, which can be easily adapted to various spatially discrete schemes. Our approach yields a significant improvement in performance, achieving a speed-up of up to 7 times over existing methods, especially in scenarios involving large numbers of nodes. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, we present a series of numerical experiments and a demonstration of its application to solving a real-world problem. The new method is made available as an open-source Python module, named SwiftNewton, which can be easily integrated with popular scientific computing frameworks. Our results provide a clear basis for further developing and refining our approach to tackle complex problems arising in the study of water waves.
